How AI is Changing DevOps: From Code Suggestions to Auto-Remediation
event.description:
Abstract As DevOps matures, we're witnessing a paradigm shift—one where artificial intelligence is no longer just an enhancement, but a driving force. In this talk, I’ll share lessons and insights from over a decade and working on large-scale cloud-native systems at AWS, where I’ve had a front-row seat to how AI is fundamentally reshaping the DevOps lifecycle.
We'll explore how AI-powered tools are moving beyond simple static analysis to provide contextual code suggestions, intelligent pull request reviews, and even predictive CI/CD pipeline optimizations. More importantly, we’ll dive into the emerging field of auto-remediation—where AI models trained on historical telemetry and incident data can detect anomalies, pinpoint root causes, and initiate corrective actions autonomously.
This session is designed for practitioners, leaders, and architects who want a strategic yet hands-on view of how AI is changing the way we build, deploy, and operate software in the cloud—today and in the years to come. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery Online Outcomes Attendees will leave this session with: 1. A clear understanding of how AI is being integrated into modern DevOps workflows—from intelligent code suggestions to automated incident response. 2. Insights into real-world use cases and practical patterns that show where AI adds value—and where human oversight remains essential. 3. Awareness of the trade-offs, risks, and governance considerations when deploying AI-driven automation in production environments. 4. Strategic considerations for teams and organizations preparing to adopt AI-enhanced DevOps practices. 5. Whether you're exploring AI for the first time or already deploying it in operations, this talk aims to bridge the technical and strategic dimensions of an increasingly intelligent DevOps landscape. Prerequisites This session is best suited for attendees with a foundational understanding of DevOps practices, cloud infrastructure, and software development lifecycles. Familiarity with CI/CD pipelines, monitoring/observability tools, and basic machine learning concepts will help participants fully engage with the content. While the talk draws on real-world experience, knowledge of any specific services is not required—key concepts will be explained with general applicability in mind. Attendees from diverse professional backgrounds are welcome too—whether you're an academic researching AI applications, a practitioner building cloud-native systems, or a government or nonprofit technologist looking to future-proof infrastructure operations. The talk is structured to ensure accessibility for non-experts while providing deeper technical insight for experienced professionals.

event.title: Harnessing the power of AIRR supercomputers for trusted research
event.description:
Abstract How can we use the country's most powerful supercomputers for research on sensitive data while keeping that data secure?
Complex AI models trained on large datasets are having a enormous impact in many research domains. However, training and applying such models requires high performance hardware and specialist accelerators such as GPUs. The new AI Research Resource (AIRR) has greatly expanded the availability of GPU-enabled compute to support large scale AI research in the UK.
Working with sensitive data requires high levels of security to ensure that the data is only accessible by approved researchers, and only for approved research. Trusted Research Environments (TREs) provide secure analysis environments for working safely with sensitive data. However, TREs do not provide the computational power and scaling that is required for the development and application of large models. Conversely, high performance computing (HPC) platforms do not generally support TRE capabilities, and therefore cannot provide sufficient security for working with sensitive data.
In FRIDGE we are building a SATRE and NHS standards compliant, cross-platform TRE on AIRR; unlocking the power of these system for AI-driven research using sensitive data.
In our talk we will discuss,
* The unique challenges of creating a secure enclave on a shared resource * How we approach the problem of building a TRE to be transferable between multiple HPC systems, and clouds, using IAC and Kubernetes * How FRIDGE can be used to add new capabilities to existing TREs * Enforcing security through policy as code * How we solve governance, when responsibility is shared between the HPC site and TRE operator * The different TRE architectures we considered, and how we arrived at our choice Acknowledgements Funded by DAREUK Phase 2 https://dareuk.org.uk/news-and-events/18-million-for-dare-uk-to-support-secure-research-on-sensitive-data/
A collaboration between The Alan Turing Institute, University College London Advanced Research Computing Centre, University of Bristol/Isambard-AI and University of Cambridge/Dawn Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes We aim to share recent progress in trusted research infrastructure. For researchers, we hope this will open new opportunities for them to bring high performance computing to their work with sensitive data. We will show how FRIDGE can be deployed stand-alone or be used as an add-on component to existing environments. We invite TRE operators to use and build upon our work, integrating it with their own trusted research deployments. Prerequisites Our talk should be of interest to everyone involved with research projects, whether that is as researchers, project managers, RSEs or another role. It will be of particular interest to people working in areas where sensitive data is important, including health, government and social science. People who are interested in TREs, HPC, or cloud computing and who use IAC or Kubernetes will get the most out of the more technical aspects of the talk. However, we will avoid in depth discussion of the low-level details of our work and not assume knowledge of the specific tools we have used. This talk should be accessible to the broad RSECon audience.

event.title: From demos to dependability: Practical evaluation strategies for AI applications
event.description:
Abstract The advent of Generative AI has transformed how we build AI models and software, but the speed we gain comes at a cost. Large language models (LLMs) let us add "intelligence" to an app in minutes, yet most prototypes stall before production because no one trusts their behaviour. We trace the shift from the traditional data-first, then model pipeline to today’s app-first, then API workflow and explain why it leaves teams blind, often without benchmark datasets or KPIs to judge performance.
The talk presents ways Research Software Engineers can close this gap by making evaluation a first-class citizen. We survey three families of evaluation for AI applications: manual prototypes, data-gathering tools, and synthetic benchmark generation, giving an overview of the field. We do a deep dive into the latest research and reflect on lessons learned over the past few years. To ground the theory, we walk through concrete examples from our own projects.
Attendees will leave with practical insights for matching evaluation strategy to project maturity, regulatory constraints, and available resources. Evaluation has become the critical bottleneck and RSEs are uniquely placed to turn it into an enabler for reproducible, sustainable science. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Participants will deepen their understanding of effective quality assurance techniques for AI-driven applications. Key outcomes include: Recognising why manual testing alone is not enough for a sustainable development with AI. Designing and selecting appropriate evaluation methods tailored to project maturity and regulatory constraints. Participants will be equipped with concrete examples of effective evaluation methods, enabling them to advocate for rigorous evaluation practices within their research groups and organisations. Prerequisites Attendees should understand basic software testing and version control. Prior exposure to Python or similar scripting languages, and a high-level idea of how Machine Learning and Large Language Models (LLMs) work is useful but not mandatory. Brief introductions to relevant concepts (LLMs, ML, evaluation) will be provided to ensure broad accessibility. The session will include introductory content to ensure all participants can engage effectively, regardless of their prior expertise.

event.title: HPC Carpentry
event.description:
Abstract The HPC Carpentry project aims to develop highly interactive workshop training materials to empower novices to effectively leverage HPC to solve scientific and technical problems in their domains. This talk provides an overview of the project and its history, explores the content and delivery of HPC Carpentry workshops, and summarises the community's plans for the future.
Modeled after The Carpentries training programs, the project’s goal is to develop foundational HPC skills and a sense of empowerment, rather than expertise. The workshop setting provides learners with hands-on experience that elicits confidence working with HPC systems and provides sufficient vocabulary to make subsequent self-study more effective.
In a major milestone, the steering committee is leading HPC Carpentry through the formal incubation process to become an official lesson program of The Carpentries, a global community teaching essential data and software skills for research. If adopted, HPC Carpentry will join the existing Software, Data, and Library Carpentry programs. This achievement is the product of significant work over the past several years, incorporating valuable materials from many contributors.
Our most recent focus has been developing materials for a user workshop. We begin with an introduction to the command-line shell (using Software Carpentry’s Unix Shell lesson), followed by our Introduction to HPC lesson, covering remote access and resource management. We end with a newly developed lesson on HPC workflow management, which walks learners through the execution of a scaling study on an HPC system, emphasizing both the benefits and limitations of the system for domain applications. This workshop program was recently run in full at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.
Future plans include building a developer workshop, reconnecting with disparate contributors, and engaging with the broader community through regular open conference calls and outreach. Acknowledgements The work described in the talk was made possible by the contributions of every HPC Carpentry community member. Thank you! The abstract was adapted from a previous conference submission, prepared by Andrew Reid, Trevor Keller, Alan O'Cais, Annajiat Alim Rasel, Wirawan Purwanto, Jane Herriman, and Benson Muite. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Audience members will leave the talk with insight into the HPC Carpentry project, ideas for how they can get involved with hosting or delivering workshops, and other ways they could contribute. They will also gain insight into the pathways through which a small, dedicated community project can join a larger existing effort and the benefits and implications of following that path. Prerequisites The talk will be accessible to all conference participants familiar with foundational concepts and terminology of high-performance/cluster computing. It will be especially relevant to those with experience of or interest in teaching HPC skills specifically, and/or open source, community-led training more generally.

event.title: Gutenberg: A Training Platform for RSEs
event.description:
Abstract Gutenberg is an interactive training platform developed by RSEs for delivering training in software engineering and research computing related topics to researchers, students and other RSEs. It is built with a modern web stack, featuring a dynamic Next.js frontend and a robust API-driven backend. Gutenberg is open-sourced and permissively licensed, making it easy to adapt, extend, and deploy.
This walkthrough will introduce the core components of the system and demonstrate how it can support material authors, learners and instructors.
1. Authors develop course content purely in Markdown, with the addition of some custom callouts, to be stored in one or more separate Git repositories, allowing easy version control and collaboration. The platform renders this material into navigable courses with embedded challenges, code blocks, comment threads, and other multimedia content.
2. Learners can browse available courses, enroll in them, and track their progress. Challenges let learners test their understanding, while embedded comment threads provide space for discussion and clarification both amongst peers and with instructors.
3. Instructors and admins have access to an extended interface where they can design and schedule events, monitor learner progress, see feedback, and respond to and resolve questions and comments.
We'll also briefly walk through how to set up and deploy your own Gutenberg instance. With configuration options and a containerized setup, it's easy to run a local or hosted version for your own or shared training materials, whether you're working individually or as part of a team. Acknowledgements Development of Gutenberg and the creation of training material was carried out under the UNIVERSE-HPC project, funded through the SPF ExCALIBUR programme under grant number EP/W035731/1 Authors
Event Type Walkthrough In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes An understanding of how to deploy, manage and utilise your own training platform as well as what benefits that brings over existing solutions. Prerequisites No prerequisites required, walkthrough should not be technical as will be more focused on the why and what of the tool rather than the implementations.

event.title: Project management beyond the process: How do RSE team leads learn what the role requires?
event.description:
Abstract Research today cannot take place without Digital Research Infrastructure (DRI). But how are the teams that develop the research software which underpins DRI managed, and how do we ensure that those leading the teams have the right skills to make them effective and inclusive leaders?
There is a wealth of technical training material targeted at researchers, Research Software Engineers and other Research Technical Professionals (RTPs). Much of this material is open and freely accessible, and institutional RSE groups now play a large role in upskilling practitioners, as disseminated at RSECon. At the same time, through the UNIVERSE-HPC project, we are aware that this availability of training material doesn’t directly translate into a more skilled and capable workforce.
A particular gap that has been identified is the lack of training materials aimed at teams developing research software, including helping those new to managing or leading diverse teams. There are a large number of resources on software project management, and general team management, but few which take into account the particular challenges of working in the research environment.
This talk will present work that DRIFT (a follow-up to UNIVERSE-HPC) has done to identify the existing resources, approaches and audiences, and understand what adaptations might be required to be able to use existing materials in a research software engineering context. Starting with the goal of teaching project management skills as they can be applied to software development in research environments, we would like to get feedback from participants on a curriculum, in particular to identify any “hidden” objectives, such as enabling inclusive leadership and research integrity. This will contribute to an openly licensed course that will be piloted in 2026, focusing on the challenges of working with teams with different experience levels, promoting effective communication and knowledge transfer, and creating positive working environments. Acknowledgements This work has been funded by the UKRI Digital Research Infrastructure programme through grant UKRI298 for the DRI-focussed training for research facilitators and teams (DRIFT) project. We thank all the other members of the DRIFT team: including Weronika Filinger, Laura Moran, Anna Roubíčková, Darren White, Martin Robinson, Jeremy Cohen, and Eirini Zormpa, as well others working in the same area who have provided input and feedback: Tracy Teal, Toby Hodges, Sarah Jaffa and Steve Crouch. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Attendees will gain a general understanding of the current landscape of training for research software project management, and a specific understanding of the work that the DRIFT project is doing to construct a curriculum and identify existing resources. They may also gain insight into how to identify gaps in their own knowledge around project management and develop a suitable learning pathway. We expect this presentation to be of interest to anyone who is associated with a research software project in any role. No prior knowledge or experience of project management is required, though this will primarily benefit those developing research software in teams rather than as individuals. Prerequisites This presentation does not require any prerequisite skills or knowledge. Attendees may benefit from having experience of being involved in research software development projects, particularly if they have been part of a development team.

event.title: Automated CI/CD with GitHub Actions, starting from scratch
event.description:
Abstract Have you ever developed a piece of code, pushed it to a GitHub repository main branch, and then moved on to other things? How do you ensure that the code remains functional in a few months’ time, when various dependencies have updated? How do you go about assigning a version number to allow clear traceability of issues for your users? And once you have released a version, how do you go about automatically deploying that to a package repository; ensuring easy installation for your userbase?
In this walkthrough, we will take a basic software tool as an example and answer these questions (and more) by incrementally building up Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery (CI/CD) workflows using the ubiquitous GitHub Actions platform.
Workflows will be developed in a live demonstration. Among other things, we will show you how to automate testing, packaging and deployment for a range of triggers (e.g. updates to a pull request). We will explore the Marketplace for some of the reusable actions that you can embed in your own workflows. We will also talk about some of the pitfalls you will encounter if you don’t release regular versions of your code, and make the case for using CI/CD regardless of the size and reach of your codebase. Authors
Event Type Walkthrough In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Following the walkthrough, attendees will grasp the principles of CI/CD, why it is helpful for ensuring the robustness of software, and be able to replicate the workflows for their own code bases. Prerequisites Familiarity with version control and the GitHub interface would be helpful. While the walkthrough will focus on a software tool written in Python, the general CI/CD workflows covered will be applicable more generally. Due to the introductory nature of the material, it will be of most benefit to those without much (if any) experience of CI/CD. However, the principles are universal enough to benefit attendees from a range of backgrounds and experience levels, whether a project manager working with a team of RSEs or a beginner programmer wanting to enhance their own tools.

event.title: Pre-commit to better code
event.description:
Abstract In this walkthrough, I will walk through using pre-commit to make your code better. Pre-commit, along with automated linters and type checkers, enforces guidelines on every commit, from stylistic issues such as whitespaces and indents, to automatically checking your code for common errors, such as missing imports or incorrect types. In collaborative projects, pre-commit can be invaluable in ensuring that the codebase is of a uniform quality. Authors
Event Type Walkthrough In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Attendees will be introduced to the pre-commit tool that can automate best practices in software development before pushing to a remote version control system such as GitHub. This tool is particularly useful when collaborating with others in enforcing agreed upon coding standards. In addition, I will cover common pre-commit rules for Python, such as linting, autoformatting and type checking. Prerequisites Walkthroughs will be in Python, but should be useful to anyone with programming experience. Knowledge of basic shell and git commands (such as git commit) is required.

event.title: Discovering Academic Open Source:- Universities don't know how much they contribute to the OS ecosystem, why is this and what can we do about it?
event.description:
Abstract Open Source is created and consumed everywhere. Many companies have good insights of what open source code is developed, contributed and used internally. This is not the case for universities. In recent years, researchers have released and contributed to lots of open source software, mostly motivated by Open Science movements (Open Data, FAIR principles, reproducibility networks), but universities don’t know what activity is happening in their university or how much impact that software is having.
Moreover, there may not be a motivation for researchers or students to share their open source activity. For example, the impact of open source contribution may not help their career progression as compared with research publications.
In this BoF session, participants will discuss what to consider when measuring open source involvement (including beyond code) in a university or research institution. We will examine what techniques are currently being employed to measure open source activity by academic Open Source Program Offices (OSPOs) globally, what are potential benefits and drawbacks of making this visible, and efforts that are being put in place to recognise and reward the social and economic impact of open source research outputs. Acknowledgements The proposers would like to thank all those who contribute to the global RSE body of knowledge, and those who participate in the CURIOSS, SustainOSS and CHAOSS communities. This session will build on the great work that they have all done to date. Authors
Event Type Birds of a Feather In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Although this session will focus on academic open source, the impact of open source research outputs has the potential to reach across sectors, for example: forming the basis of spin-outs, forming part of the products of public-private consortia research projects, or being adopted or modified by governments or interested individuals around the world. The challenge of measuring open source activity in a university is also an interesting topic for anyone who is familiar with open source ecosystems to explore the differences and similarities between open source in academia and other contexts. Prerequisites This 90 minute session will be suitable for all attendees who have an interest in this space. No prior knowledge of the topic is essential, but a basic knowledge of what open source software is would be helpful.

event.title: From code to contributions: exploring open source culture in academia
event.description:
Abstract "It is a truth universally acknowledged that a code repository with an open source license must be in want of an extra maintainer." - Jane Austen, probably.
While academic researchers and research technical professionals rely heavily on open source tools and software, and open research policies increase the amount of codebases available globally, contribution patterns remain uneven, with maintenance work often undervalued within academic reward structures. This workshop forms part of a larger 2025 SSI Fellowship projecct examining the current culture of open source contributions in the academic landscape and considering opportunities to incentivise, reward, and recongise the collective work of maintaining

They will also hear from groups currently working to actively promote open source contributions at their organisations, before brainstorming and developing practical proposals for effective support for open source contributions within academic settings.
Participants will leave with both individual action commitments and collective strategies to enhance the recognition, support, and sustainability of open source contributions in academic environments. Quick tips for making your software outlive your job
event.description:
Abstract Loss of key personnel has always been a risk for research software projects. Key members of a team may have to step away due to a change in national or university funding, due to illness or burnout, or because they are simply changing jobs. Today, political and financial changes are putting large numbers of researchers out of work simultaneously, both in the UK and abroad, potentially leaving large amounts of research software abandoned and destabilising necessary digital research infrastructure. We present ten tips to help researchers ensure that the software they have built will continue to be usable after they have left their present job, for any reason. These techniques, methods, and best practices were collectively sourced from researchers from dozens of universities across the globe, and are now being improved upon in a ReSA Task Force. The tips shown here will enable individual researchers and labs to position their work in a way that makes it more sustainable and usable going forward, resulting in a more resilient research software ecosystem. event.title: flowR: Program Slicing and Dependency Analysis to Improve the Reuse of R Scripts
event.description:
Abstract A program slicer reduces a program to only the parts relevant to a certain variable of interest like a visualization or a statistical test. This way, a slice is usually a much smaller script that is easier to understand, has fewer dependencies, and focuses only on the analysis of interest.Such slices can be beneficial for both reviewers, trying to understand and validate the methodology, and authors wishing to reuse and reproduce existing analyses. Even if the original script is not executable due to missing dependencies, a slice that does not rely on them can be executed and reused independently.In our talk, we introduce flowR, a novel program slicer and dataflow analyzer for R, alongside its Visual Studio Code extension and RStudio addin which allow users to interactively slice their scripts directly from their IDE.To calculate slices and the dependency information, flowR uses a pipeline architecture that first parses the R code into an abstract syntax tree, which is subsequently normalized into a version-independent intermediate representation.Based on this representation, flowR uses an interprocedural dataflow analysis to construct a static dataflow graph of the entire script.This graph describes the dependencies of variables and function calls, compensating for the inherently dynamic nature of R.A program slice is essentially the subgraph that is reachable from the variable of interest.
Besides slicing, we also provide a dependency view of the entire analysis script which shows the inputs, sourced files, required libraries, and produced outputs to help users find and understand the important parts and required inputs. Acknowledgements This work was supported by the German Research Foundation (DFG): 504226141 Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Attendees will learn about program slicing and dataflow analysis, and how it can be used to improve the quality of R scripts. They will learn how to use flowR to slice R scripts and visualize the dataflow graph. They will also learn about the benefits of using flowR in their own work, and how it can be integrated into their workflow. Prerequisites This talk is targeted at researchers who are using R for their work - however, as program slicing and dependency analysis work for any language, the concepts may be of interest to any researcher. Yet, to follow the examples a basic understanding of R is beneficial. We assume no prior knowledge of program slicing or dataflow analysis.

event.title: Shinyscholar – a template for creating reproducible Shiny applications in R
event.description:
Abstract Shiny is a framework for producing apps in R that is an increasingly popular method for academics to develop software. However a survey of apps published in 2023 found they typically fail to facilitate reproducible research or provide attribution to software developers.
Additionally, academics often have little formal training in software development and consequently apps fail to adhere to best practices in structuring code and automated testing. To address these shortcomings, we present Shinyscholar (https://cran.r-project.org/package=shinyscholar) as a framework built upon Shiny which provides a suite of features tailored to the production of academic Shiny apps.
Developed by forking WallaceEcoMod (an app for modelling species distributions with many desirable features) and the addition of extra features, Shinyscholar generates a template app structured as an R package where an analysis is broken down into steps with multiple options for each step. Analyses from generated apps can be saved and loaded at any point, a file can be downloaded that completely reproduces the analysis and developers of dependent software are appropriately cited.
Other features include a flexible system for reporting messages to users, structures for providing user guidance, the ability to view source code from inside the application and a walk-through to guide new users. The visible structure of the app is reflected in the structure of the code, with each possible option in the analysis composed of a Shiny module that calls one function, facilitating maintenance and automated testing.
The talk will explain how to create a new app and the workflow for developing modules. By using Shinyscholar, to create an app, developers can concentrate on creating domain-specific functionality rather than enabling communication between modules or designing user interfaces and will be more able to produce apps that follow best practices, are maintainable, and run reliably. Acknowledgements Shinyscholar was created by forking WallaceEcoMod and we are grateful for those developers for creating much of the functionality. Funding to develop Shinyscholar was provided by Wellcome. Additional information I'm happy to present a more technical workshop instead of a talk if that would be of interest / helpful. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Attendees will learn how Shinyscholar solves common problems in scientific shiny apps and how to use Shinyscholar to create new apps. Those new to Shiny will learn how it can help to disseminate methods more widely. For attendees will basic understanding of Shiny they will learn about advanced topics such as modules, testing and asynchronous programming. Prerequisites Some experience of R would be helpful, but the talk will start from the basics of what a shiny app is and how they work before moving on to discuss the problems that Shinyscholar solves. The content will be high-level and not get bogged down in the technical details.

event.title: Can others reproduce your results? Recipes for using uv and pixi to manage Python dependencies
event.description:
Abstract Reproducible environments are crucial for ensuring consistent and reliable software development. They enable RSEs to recreate exact configurations, facilitating the long-term maintenance of projects that may include collaborators with varied levels of software engineering experience. But they're not always easy to achieve. In the worst case scenario, a complicated or difficult pathway during the setup of a project make the whole thing inaccessible to entry-level coders.
This walkthrough will demonstrate the common pitfalls experienced when using pip or conda alone (package conflicts, inconsistent state, and the inability to work across platforms and architectures), and use these to motivate a desire for something better. It will then explore how environment management tools like uv and pixi can help. It will include practical steps and examples of how an RSE, data scientist or scientific coder might incorporate them into a project. The sharing of advice and experiences of attendees would also be welcome!
This walkthrough will be of interest to people that use pip or conda/mamba to install packages for a Python project, or a more established tool like poetry, Pipenv or pip-tools. It will be especially useful to people that collaborate with researchers that have less software engineering experience, but still need to run and develop the project. event.title: A Context for Requirements Handling in an Agile Workflow
event.description:
Abstract When King’s Digital Lab (KDL), an RSE unit based in the Faculty of Arts and Humanities at King’s College London, began operations in 2016 we quickly adopted the industry-standard DSDM Agile methodology. Its emphasis on a fixed-time-and-cost basis with flexibility on features aligns well with the grant-funded projects work we commonly do. Our SDLC includes DSDM-recommended steps and documentation which we have found very helpful. However, because we have small solution development (SDT) teams each working on several projects simultaneously, workflows can be complex and it has been challenging to fully and consistently follow Agile precepts, especially with respect to handling project requirements.
We like the theory of moving from initial high-level requirement descriptions to greater specificity via iterative development but in practice have found that while a typical Agile try/asses/adjust/try again fosters creativity and refinement in implementation it also brings a constant risk of confusion and inefficiency for the SDT. We have come to see that fast-paced iteration demands a fixed context: something consistent, intuitive, and convenient that allows both SDT and project partners to produce and keep track of evolving requirement descriptions and the constantly moving parts - discussions, decisions, task creation, etc. - that surround them. ‘Context’ here is not quite an approach (as, for instance, Specification by Example), or a formalized set of practices (like the Requirements Development & Management Practice Area of CMMI), or a purpose-built software tool (e,g. Altium 365) but might incorporate aspects from any or all those things.
Drawing from our experience at KDL this talk will firstly discuss specific issues in requirements handling which can thwart Agility and frustrate all parties in a project. It will then set out aims, principles and practical considerations pertinent to a fixed context that facilitates rapid iteration in an environment of multiple complex workflows. Acknowledgements Colleagues at King's Digital Lab, King's College London, and in particular Senior Research Software Engineer Geoffroy Noël with whom I have had many helpful conversations on the subject of the talk. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Whilst the talk arises from project experience at KDL - which as a humanities-based RSE group occupies a particular niche in the overall RSE landscape – the overall topic of requirements handling and the specific issues discussed should resonate with any RSE trying to put Agile theory into practice. The main takeaway is that for RSE teams employing Agile methodology, efficient requirements handling needs an enabling context which must be in place before the work starts. It is precisely because requirements evolve during the rapid prototyping/feedback iterations of an Agile approach that it is vital to keep track of all important aspects of the requirements. There can be no ‘one size fits all’ implementation of a context – teams will adapt their own preferred (or enforced) approaches, standards and software tools – but there are common aims and principles underpinning the context. Prerequisites No detailed prior knowledge is required. Many audience members will know something about the core concepts of Agile software development methodologies and they will not need to have specific experience to appreciate the relevant problems / solutions that the talk will discuss.

event.title: From open science goals to technical implementation: Enabling sustainable data sharing for a research team
event.description:
Abstract In this talk, we will present how as RSEs we helped a research team achieve part of their open science goals.
A group of researchers studying the generation of scientific knowledge for socio-ecological sustainability sought to share with the public a 5.5-million-row dataset they created during a three-year project in an accessible and engaging way. While their initial expectation was to create a dashboard using Shiny for R, it soon became clear that the nature of the dataset, the financial constraints of the project, and the target audience required a broader approach.
During the talk, we will discuss how we approached the process of understanding their needs, managing expectations, and devising a sustainable solution. We will also share some of the technical decisions made to that end, such as restructuring the data for efficient querying, precomputing summary tables, implementing interface logic that dynamically adjusted the level of granularity based on user interaction, and developing a companion R package. These design decisions balanced usability with long-term maintainability, ensuring that the tool could remain available beyond the end of the research funding.
This experience illustrates how RSEs contribute not only code, but also strategic thinking that bridges open research goals with the technical realities of implementation. By aligning design decisions with open science principles and practical constraints, RSEs can help ensure that research outputs are not just published, but also usable, reusable, and impactful over time. Acknowledgements The research project "Social Networks and Socio-ecological Sustainability Project" (FONDECYT No. 1220560) was funded by the Chilean National Research and Development Agency (ANID). Its principal investigator is Julien Vanhulst, from Universidad Católica del Maule, in Chile. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Participants will learn from a concrete experience implementing a data-sharing solution that remains usable and maintainable beyond a research project’s funding period. Attendees will leave with practical takeaways on how to ensure that tools like dashboards—and the underlying data processing workflows—remain functional, accessible, and aligned with open science goals even after RSE involvement and funding have ended. Prerequisites Although the solution presented here makes use of R + Shiny + GitHub, the talk doesn’t focus primarily on the code itself, but on the workflows and technical decisions (also, Shiny works in Python, so the takeaways are transferable).

event.title: Reflections on cross-cutting software tools born out of project work
event.description:
Abstract RSEs regularly collaborate on time-bounded projects, with code ownership remaining with researchers. Sometimes, however, such collaborations lead to the development of cross-cutting digital research infrastructure with potential for impact beyond a single project or domain.
How can RSEs identify and nurture these pieces of software, and how can they use their unique position in research to drive these interconnections?
ICCS RSEs work with climate scientists to improve the functionality and sustainability of climate modelling code. Much of this is written in Fortran, which remains relevant due to continued updates to the language standards and compilers, and considerable societal inertia, but lacks native support for machine learning (ML). With hybrid modelling being a popular research topic, a common request from collaborators is to facilitate inter-operation of their codebases with the popular ML package PyTorch. As a result we developed the FTorch interface. Given the cross-cutting nature of ML inter-operation, FTorch was spun out of the original project as a fully-fledged package in its own right and has since been deployed in several other projects and domains.
In this talk, we reflect on our experiences developing FTorch. We discuss the decision to spin FTorch out beyond the original collaboration, and the subsequent journey to become an independent package developed and maintained by our team. Early on we faced the challenge of developing FTorch in ‘non-project time’ and managing it in-house (something not generally within ICCS’ remit for project work). We subsequently secured FTorch-specific funding to support development, promotion, and collaboration. Finally, we discuss how the unique role of the RSE is well suited to spotting opportunities for interconnected research.
We hope that the talk will inspire attendees to focus on cross-cutting software that they have developed in their team and provide useful tips for how to grow such software into fully-fledged projects. Acknowledgements We acknowledge the valuable contributions of all current and past FTorch developers and contributors.
ICCS is supported by Schmidt Sciences, LLC.
This project was supported with funding from the Cambridge Centre for Data-Driven Discovery and Accelerate Programme for Scientific Discovery, made possible by a donation from Schmidt Sciences. Authors

We hope that such outcomes could be beneficial to all RSEs who develop software within their organisation, whether as part of project work or to support specific tasks. Prerequisites Awareness of machine learning and/or Fortran would be helpful but not necessary (we will not discuss technical details in this talk).

event.title: Building Robust Practices for Research Outputs: Supporting Quality and Assessment
event.description:
Abstract Research Software Engineering (RSE) is no longer a hidden force behind scientific discovery—it is a cornerstone of research excellence. As modern research becomes increasingly computational, the role of RSEs has evolved from coding assistants to essential contributors who drive innovation, ensure reproducibility, and elevate the quality of scientific outputs.
Departing from the experience of an embedded RSE team in the arts and humanities, this talk explores the dual identity of RSEs: as both enablers of high-impact research and as integral components of human digital research infrastructure.
Central to this discussion are two lightweight but powerful tools: the KDL Checklist Document for digital outputs assessment and the Project Release Document (PRD). The Checklist is a practical tool meant for academic colleagues to guide them through a holistic assessment of their digital output when submitting to the UK research evaluation framework (REF). The PRD is meant to be used internally by a KDL project sub-team to ensure the overall suitability of the digital output ahead of its release.
These documents are meant to guide the King’s Digital Lab team and its partners through critical development milestones, ensuring that research software and associated outputs are not only functional, but also reproducible, maintainable, and robust. From versioning and documentation to testing and licensing, these tools embed best practices directly into the release process and review of outputs. The talk will also reflect on the difficulties encountered when introducing new practices and how to best socialise them both internally and with partners.
By framing RSE as infrastructure, we acknowledge the people, practices, and principles that underpin trustworthy research. This perspective elevates the conversation beyond code quality to institutional and lab or departmental-level strategy— where integrating RSE good practices translates into investment in research reliability, scalability, and long-term impact. Acknowledgements We would like to acknowledge authors and reviewers of the two documented presented in this talk. Both the KDL Checklist Document for digital outputs assessment and the Project Release Document were developed at the King’s Digital Lab. We would like to acknowledge the other members of our team that have been involved in the authorship and the review of both:

Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Attendees will gain a clear understanding of how Research Software Engineering (RSE) practices directly support research excellence and long-term impact. They will leave with practical knowledge of how to apply the Checklist and Project Release Documents to ensure robust, reproducible software and associated digital outputs releases. The session will offer actionable insights for both individuals and teams—whether you are an experienced RSE, a researcher managing code, or part of an organisation looking to formalise software practices. Participants will also develop a broader perspective on RSE as human digital infrastructure, helping them advocate for sustainable software roles and processes within their institutions. By blending technical guidance with strategic framing, the session aims to inspire attendees across sectors and skill levels to adopt practices that elevate the quality, reliability, and visibility of research software and associated digital outputs. Prerequisites This session is designed for research software engineers, developers, project managers, and technical leads who are involved in building, maintaining, or releasing research software and related digital outputs. While some familiarity with software development processes (e.g., version control, testing, documentation) will help attendees get the most from the session, the concepts presented will be accessible to those newer to research software engineering but interested in how to embed robust RSE processes in production and acceptance phases as well as in submissions of high quality digital outputs to the REF for HEIs sector. We will clearly define all terminology and include practical examples that illustrate the real-world application of tools like the Checklist and Project Release Documents. Those interested in embedding robust, sustainable practices into their workflows—and in understanding how RSEs function as a strategic component of research infrastructure—will find this session particularly valuable.

event.title: The Journal of Open Source Software
event.description:
Abstract The Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS; https://joss.theoj.org) publishes short articles describing open source research software. The review process is open, iterative and includes the software itself, thereby encouraging good software practice. It has published articles co-authored by RSEs and is potentially an interesting avenue through which to recognise RSE contributions to research software in formal research literature. event.title: It’s time to decarbonise digital research
event.description:
Abstract As the climate crisis intensifies the digital research community is becoming increasingly aware of its environmental responsibilities. This poster draws on a comment article which argues that while many researchers are motivated to act, grassroots enthusiasm is often hampered by a lack of clear guidance, institutional support, and coherent frameworks for meaningful change (https://tinyurl.com/bdshdk4y). This leads to a real risk of squandering goodwill, and slowing the pace of change.
To bridge this gap, community-led initiatives, certification schemes, and peer networks are emerging as powerful enablers of sustainable digital practice. This poster will showcase some promising activities in this space, including grassroots networks such as the Green Research Software Engineering Special Interest Group and NetDRIVE, as well as tools like Green DiSC. These initiatives not only provide practical guidance but also foster a sense of shared purpose across disciplines and institutions. Acknowledgements

event.title: FAIR2 for research software: developing a FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable) and reproducible research software training programme
event.description:
Abstract Recently there has been growing recognition that research software, defined as “source code files, algorithms, scripts, computational workflows and executables that were created during the research process or for a research purpose”1, should adhere to the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable) principles2, as well as meeting broader open research goals such as reproducibility. The FAIR guidelines for research software (FAIR4RS) provide a framework for the development of FAIR research software1. However, many researchers require additional support to meet these guidelines. Training in the FAIR4RS principles is needed to promote the uptake of FAIR research software practices3.
The University of Sheffield Research Software Engineering team and collaborators developed a modular training programme to support researchers in applying FAIR principles and open research practices to their research software. Topics are offered as separate modules which can be selected according to an individual’s learning goals. We aim to motivate and equip participants with the skills and knowledge needed to create and publish FAIR research software, to meet our goal to support research excellence at the university by enhancing capacity for producing high quality, efficient and sustainable research software.
So far the programme has attracted over 200 registrations and 150 attendees across the University of Sheffield, and provided over 40 hours of training, from software lifecycle planning and licensing to packaging and publishing software. Course materials have been developed as open educational resources under Creative Commons licensing. Feedback from participants indicates that this training is timely and relevant to researchers’ needs.
1 Barker et al., 2022, ‘Introducing the FAIR Principles for Research Software’.
2 Wilkinson et al., 2016, ‘The FAIR Guiding Principles for Scientific Data Management and Stewardship’.
3 Barker et al., 2024, ‘The FAIR for Research Software Principles after two years’. Acknowledgements The training programme was created by the Research Software Engineering team, in collaboration with the Data Analytics Service and the Library team at the University of Sheffield, supported by the School of Computer Science, the School of Mathematical and Physical Sciences and IT Services—Research & Innovation IT. Course materials were developed by Jenni Adams, Farhad Allain, Dan Brady, Ric Campbell, Joe Heffer, Kate O’Neill, Neil Shephard, Romain Thomas, Sylvia Whittle, and Christopher Wild. Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes This poster will be of interest to individuals who are involved in training researchers in better research software practices or who work in settings where research outputs include software. Attendees will gain insight into the motivation behind creating a FAIR4RS training programme, the process of developing the programme and course materials, and the impact of delivering the programme to researchers at a research-intensive university. Attendees will be able to access online course materials via a QR code. Prerequisites No specialist skills or knowledge are required. The poster will introduce the FAIR4RS guidelines to enable everyone to engage with the poster’s subject matter.

event.title: Developing the enCore Community Land Model (eCLM): Adapting Community Land Model version 5 (CLM5) to fit into modular Earth system simulation platforms
event.description:
Abstract The enCore Community Land Model (eCLM) is a Fortran-based HPC software for simulating the biogeophysical, biogeochemical, and hydrological processes on Earth's land surface. These physical processes are derived from the Community Land Model version 5 (CLM5)—a land surface model developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research in USA. While eCLM take most of its scientific features from CLM5, it differs mainly in its software architecture, which has been designed to readily integrate into a modular Earth system modeling platform. This presentation showcases the software refactoring efforts involved in transforming CLM5, a mature HPC software for land surface modelling, into eCLM. Notably, this RSE work contributes to a larger ongoing effort towards a next-generation modular Earth system modeling platform. eCLM was initiated in 2020 and is being constantly tested (e.g. through continuous integration and deployment practices) and improved (e.g. by introducing new modelling features such as vegetation processes and land management) to serve the research activities at the Agrosphere Institute in Jülich Research Centre, Germany. event.title: Bridging Bench and Code: RSEs Driving Omics
event.description:
Abstract Life sciences research is increasingly reliant on both data and software. Even traditionally experimental research groups are requiring efficient, robust programming solutions while engaging in complex data manipulation. While commercial tech and sequencing companies do offer bioinformatics services, these are often too far removed from the specific scientific questions posed by principal investigators (PIs).
There are many areas within biological research known as "omics", including genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and epigenomics. "Omics" refers to large-scale studies of biological molecules, aiming to comprehensively characterise and quantify them. Advances in sequencing and other high-throughput technologies over recent years lead to the development of new omics databases and datasets generated from laboratory-based research – this offers an excellent opportunity for Research Software Engineers (RSEs) to contribute meaningfully, combining data manipulation, software development, and domain-specific insights to make a significant impact and actively shape research outcomes.
RSEs can play a critical role bridging the gap between benchwork and software development. This involves not only engaging with the code, but also with the science itself by designing solutions grounded in experimental reality. Such collaboration has the potential to foster meaningful scientific partnerships. Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes This poster aims to demystify omics research for RSEs by connecting biological concepts to real computational challenges. It will also showcase the current opportunities within lab-based research groups for RSEs to make impactful contributions. Prerequisites No specific prerequisites are necessary. A general interest in research software, reproducibility, or life sciences. The poster is intended to be accessible to attendees with a general interest in research software, reproducibility, or life sciences, whether they are new to the field or experienced RSEs.

event.title: Enabling Research Software Excellence through RSEng Community Conversations
event.description:
Abstract A six-month-long online community conversation series titled "Enabling Open Science Through Research Code" (https://rse-asia.github.io/RSE_Asia/events.html) was organised jointly by the RSE Asia and RSSE Africa communities from October 2024 to March 2025. Drawing inspiration from CodeRefinery’s (https://coderefinery.org/) training materials, the series was contextualised for the communities in the Global South. Since, in the Global South, the open science movement is comparatively more recognised than the research software engineering (RSE) movement, the message was anchored in the language of open science to broaden reach and engagement among researchers who code.
Each episode featured an open panel discussion on a topic critical to sustainable and reproducible research software practices, such as reproducibility, documentation, and testing. People working in the Asian and African regions or those who had experience working/collaborating with researchers from these regions were invited as panellists. To enhance accessibility, the sessions were recorded and shared with the communities. Each episode was also accompanied by a summary blog post and a curated resource sheet publicly available on Zenodo.
The impact of the series was visible in community engagement, with RSE Asia’s social media (https://www.linkedin.com/company/rse-asia-association/?viewAsMember=true) engagement rate increasing by 71% during the process. The series also enjoyed popularity with a globally distributed audience across varied time zones.
This poster presents the model that was used for organising this Global South focused community initiative, the strategies that were adopted to increase participation and accessibility, and the types of openly licensed outputs that were co-created. Overall, this series is a testament to how cross-regional collaboration and community-driven efforts can effectively promote research software excellence. event.title: Reimagining Digital Accessibility: From Compliance to Collective Responsibility at King's Digital Lab
event.description:
Abstract Digital accessibility is often seen as a compliance issue, but King’s Digital Lab’s experience shows it is deeply rooted in human connection, team dynamics, and strategic thinking. We share our current approach to embedding accessibility within research software projects. Informed by years of learning and feedback, the updated process is designed to be both practical and collaborative, ensuring accessibility is actively considered across software development roles and project phases, encouraging shared ownership across disciplines.
In 2023, we formed a dedicated accessibility team involving a designer, engineer, and project manager to lead a procedural shift. The approach builds on lessons learnt from previous efforts and is structured around our Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), supported by shared documentation and visual artefacts, with stages aligned to clearly defined roles and responsibilities.
The process was trialed on active projects to test its usability, refine documentation, and identify areas for improvement within ongoing project workflows. This iterative rollout ensured the approach stayed responsive to real team needs, while encouraging open feedback and continuous refinement. We focused on building a process that promotes engagement, adaptability, and sustained momentum over rigid compliance.
The poster outline key principles and elements that shaped our process, offering RSE teams to reflect on, adapt, or build upon in their own contexts. Our process begins by prioritising accessibility requirements using the MoSCoW method, followed by scoping with the project team. Assessments and fixes are integrated continuously during development. Fixes are documented in GitHub; unresolved issues, tools, and methods are recorded in the accessibility statement when needed.
We welcome feedback, collaboration, and insights from others exploring inclusive, process-based strategies for accessibility in technical and research-focused environments. Our goal is to foster accessible outputs through approaches that are inclusive not just of users, but of the research software teams that create them. Acknowledgements The contributions of the King’s Digital Lab team members involved in the trial projects, as well as the valuable feedback and insights from all contributors, are gratefully acknowledged in the development of the current digital accessibility approach. Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes The poster offers practical insight into embedding accessibility within research software development by aligning inclusive practices with team structures and project phases. It presents a process-oriented approach that frames accessibility as a shared responsibility across roles. Attendees will gain strategies for integrating accessibility into their own Software Development Lifecycle using lightweight tools such as MoSCoW prioritisation, collaborative scoping, and in-sprint assessments. The poster also highlights the importance of internal feedback loops, visual documentation, and role clarity in sustaining accessibility efforts beyond compliance. Viewers will be encouraged to reflect on their own practices and explore adaptable, team-driven methods to support more inclusive research software outputs. Prerequisites Attendees will benefit from familiarity with team-based software development processes, particularly agile or evolutionary development methods. A basic understanding of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) and the challenges of implementing accessibility in digital products will provide helpful context. Experience with role-based workflows and/or documentation practices in research software settings is useful but not essential. This submission is particularly relevant to those managing legacy systems, implementing accessibility at scale, or struggling with uneven team engagement in accessibility efforts. Project managers, technical leads, developers, designers, and research software engineers engaged in building inclusive tools or platforms will find practical insights applicable to their contexts. While we reference specific tools and standards, the core focus is on strategy, collaboration, and team dynamics, making the material accessible to a broad range of technical and non-technical roles.

event.title: Green Research Software Engineering for Beginners
event.description:
Abstract This poster introduces foundational green software engineering concepts collated specifically for Research Software Engineers (RSEs) at the beginning of their sustainability journey. With computational research increasingly driving scientific discovery, understanding the environmental impact of research software has become crucial. Research computing, particularly high-performance computing (HPC) consumes significant energy resources, making sustainable practices essential.
1. We first highlight major scientific research fields that consume large amounts of compute power. 2. We then identify key energy-intensive compute processes including CPU utilisation, memory management, disk operations, and continuous integration/deployment pipelines that represent significant areas for optimisation. 3. The poster presents practical monitoring tools such as `CodeCarbon` for tracking machine learning model emissions and `AIWattch` for measuring large language model’s (LLM) environmental impacts during browser-based interactions. 4. We introduce various metrics for evaluating software energy efficiency, e.g. energy consumption per function, water usage considerations, and lifecycle assessment approaches. 5. By identifying emission scope in terms of direct (Scope 1), indirect energy-related (Scope 2), and value chain (Scope 3) impacts, we enable RSEs to make environmentally informed development decisions. 6. The poster advocates for GREENER software engineering principles that promote awareness and collaborative action toward sustainable development practices.
As use of artificial intelligence and machine learning applications is booming across research domains, this introduction provides guidance for professionals seeking to minimise the environmental footprint of their increasingly computation-intensive work. Acknowledgements
Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes Attendees will gain practical skills to measure and reduce the environmental impact of their research software. They'll leave equipped with valued sustainability expertise in scientific computing. Prerequisites Basic knowledge of software engineering process and terminologies

event.title: Developing the GOTO Telescope Control System
event.description:
Abstract The Gravitational-wave Optical Transient Observer (GOTO) is an astronomical survey project utilising a network of robotic telescopes to monitor the night sky from two sites: La Palma in the Canary Islands and Siding Spring Observatory in Australia. The GOTO Telescope Control System (G‐TeCS) is a custom robotic control system, written predominantly in Python, which autonomously manages the telescope hardware and nightly operations, as well as directing the overall observing strategy of the network. Development of the control system begun prior to the commissioning of the first GOTO prototype on La Palma in 2017, and continued through the expansion of the La Palma site in 2021 and the addition of the Australian site in 2023.
At the sites, each telescope is automated by G-TeCS through a master control program (the “pilot”), which monitors and sends commands to the hardware daemons that interface with each part of the telescope hardware (cameras, mount, dome, etc). The pilot has robust systems for monitoring external conditions to ensure the safety of the telescopes in bad weather, as well as routines to attempt recovery of the hardware should any errors occur.
Also part of G-TeCS is the central alert monitoring and scheduling system, which is hosted at Warwick University in the UK. The G-TeCS “sentinel” listens to alert streams from different astrophysical detectors and processes any new alerts into targets for the GOTO telescopes. These are then sent out to the sites by the “scheduler” system, which also monitors the telescopes and determines what they should observe between alerts.
Here we will give a brief overview of the GOTO project and the G-TeCS software, focusing on the RSE involvement and outlining the future work planned over the next two years.
