event.title: An integrated Knowledge Management System to support Open Science training
event.description:
Abstract OLS is a not-for-profit organisation, dedicated to capacity building and diversifying leadership in research worldwide (https://we-are-ols.org/). Since 2020, we have trained 400+ participants across 50+ countries in Open Science practices, with the help of 300+ mentors and experts.
We present our Knowledge Management System (KMS), a live, open‑source pipeline that connects people, data and processes to drive community impact and research‑software best practice. In this poster, you’ll see:
* Pipeline diagrams illustrating integrations between GitHub Actions, Python scripts, CiviCRM, Zotero, CSV and Jupyter for cohort coordination.
* Impact metrics visualised to show how automation frees human effort for higher‑order tasks.
* A contributor map displaying the global distribution of the OLS community.
We’ll demonstrate how the KMS, designed for transparency and collaboration, supports both Research Excellence—by embedding metadata standards and reproducibility into everyday practice—and Human Digital Research Infrastructure (DRI)—by mapping the “people layer” of software infrastructure.
Designed to reuse, our KMS integrates with open data solutions, offering a toolkit for like-minded organisations seeking to streamline workflows, credit volunteers, and scale open‑science impact. Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes The poster is tailored to be valuable for anyone who works with large open communities. This includes researchers, educators, and administrators working in academia, industry, charities, and government who are involved in open science initiatives. Attendees will learn how to design a Knowledge Management System (KMS) that promotes transparency, collaboration, and impact measurement. They will gain meaningful insights into effective strategies for managing volunteers and tracking their contributions in open science projects. Prerequisites No prior technical knowledge is required. The talk focuses on the practical application of a Knowledge Management System (KMS), not its technical intricacies. Because the session is designed to be accessible to a broad audience, we will use clear, jargon-free language and provide explanations for any technical terms used.

event.title: DRI-focussed training for research facilitators and teams (DRIFT)
event.description:
Abstract Digital Research Infrastructure (DRI) is now ubiquitous in research. It has revolutionised the way that we conduct research, pervading all aspects of the research lifecycle. From the use of large-scale computing for machine-learning and big data, to the management of experiments for record keeping and reproducibility, research is powered by the software and hardware that have become vital for modern researchers. This requires new skills and forms of research collaboration, as research supported by DRI aims at larger scales and interdisciplinary collaboration.
DRIFT aims to address the lack of DRI training for research support roles, in particular within interdisciplinary research teams, and to improve visibility of DRI outside of physical sciences and engineering. Developing support for research facilitators is particularly important, as they play a vital and trusted role in nurturing links between technical professionals and the research community, thus enhancing the impact of the skills development activities we are undertaking.
We aim to increase the impact of DRI through greater awareness and understanding, and more effective use. We have three main objectives: supporting research facilitators working within communities that could benefit from DRI offerings so that they can efficiently assist researchers understand its advantages; training research teams in skills that benefit collaboration, team science, and inter- or multi-disciplinary working; and community engagement with a wider range of research institutions and disciplines focussing on those without existing direct access to institutional HPC services. These objectives will be achieved through development of courses and other content for both research facilitators and research teams, community engagement through DRI awareness roadshows (including small demonstration HPC clusters), and the extension and improvement of the open-source Gutenberg training platform. This will improve the way that the expertise required to efficiently and effectively use DRI is developed within the research community. Acknowledgements DRIFT is funded by UKRI. Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes Attendees will benefit from wider understanding of research facilitation, the diverse forms the research facilitator role can take, and content and activities that exist and/or are being developed to support this. RSEs and technical professionals will learn about existing content and approaches that may help them deliver or develop their own training to efficiently support other researchers and users in accessing and using DRI. More experienced trainers, facilitators, or team leaders will benefit from learning about the development of a course in teaching project management skills as they can be applied to software development in research environments. There should be information about how to access suitable training for all levels! Prerequisites No specialist knowledge required; this poster should be relevant to a diverse conference audience as it relates to training and the development of training materials.

event.title: Leveraging GitHub API Data to Evaluate Git and GitHub Training Outcomes
event.description:
Abstract A key challenge in evaluating the effectiveness of technical training (e.g., Git) is assessing the real-world application of learned skills. Post-training surveys offer one assessment method but suffer from limitations such as variable response rates and limited long-term evaluation. Tracking tool usage in natural settings offers continuous and more detailed insights into application but presents implementation challenges.
The 'Git & GitHub through GitKraken Client - From Zero to Hero!' training has been delivered by the RSE Sheffield team to over 300 participants since 2016. Importantly, a core component of this training involves participants creating and merging a pull request (PR) in a dedicated repository ('evolottery'/'collaborative_github_exercise'). This hands-on exercise, while not initially for evaluation, offers a unique opportunity for naturalistic tracking of training application. Utilizing the GitHub API, we can retrieve data on these PRs (username and date) to assess participants' subsequent Git and GitHub activity.
The poster will detail findings from analysis of this cohort. Specifically, presenting changes in Github activity over time relative to training completion, and exploring the adoption of other Git/GitHub features used in the training. Finally, we will discuss the limitations of these results specifically and our methodology more generally. Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes There are two key takeaways for the audience: First, they will gain an understanding of a practical methodology for evaluating technical training outcomes, that is an alternative to traditional survey-based evaluations. Second, they will learn about the results of this project, which provides a quantitative measure of the effectiveness of the training. Prerequisites Prerequisites will be minimal. Some understanding of the technical aspects of the methodology would be beneficial, but are not essential for understanding the results.

event.title: AutoEmulate: Python library for automatically creating accurate and efficient emulators of complex simulations.
event.description:
Abstract Physical systems are understood and developed through simulations. The complexity of these systems often results in costly and time-consuming simulations. Emulators (surrogate models) can approximate the solution of simulations at a fraction of the computational expense. However, building effective emulators typically requires significant machine learning (ML) expertise, posing a barrier for domain experts. To overcome this limitation, we present AutoEmulate, a Python package that automates the construction of the best emulator suited for a given simulation, employing state-of-the-art advancements in the field. AutoEmulate supports a wide range of emulator models as well as data preprocessing, calibration, and analysis methods. AutoEmulate’s user-friendly interface enables domain experts to deploy high-performance emulators with minimal ML expertise, offering a reliable solution for simulation-driven exploration across various disciplines. Acknowledgements Alan Turing Institute Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes There is a significant number of researchers and software engineers who write code to do physical simulations but have no or little knowledge about emulators or surrogate models. Attendees will learn what an emulator is, and how AutoEmulate can be used to easily develop their own emulators. Readers will discover the main features and limitations of AutoEmulate. Readers will also learn how to contribute to rapidly growing open-source package, where a significant number of the software offerings in this space are proprietary. Prerequisites The high-level concepts are accessible for everyone. People with experience of writing software for simulations will likely understand the details and are the primary audience for the software package.

event.title: pyonb: an open-source API and optical character recognition SDK for automated document-to-text conversion of clinical records
event.description:
Abstract Optical character recognition (OCR) software is becoming increasingly prevalent with the expanding computational power and advancements in natural language processing, which enables reuse of previously untapped data due to the lack of tools for converting images into computer-readable text. Broadly, OCR is the analysis, recognition and extraction of text from documents. There are numerous open-source OCR software toolkits (Tesseract, Docling, olmOCR, PaddleOCR, Marker, Sparrow, MinerU, etc.) providing automatic conversion of images or filetypes such as PDF and DOCX into structured outputs.
Data storage is significantly heterogenous across and within UK hospitals. Medical data is often stored within data warehouses containing hundreds of millions of documents. This volume of data combined with the difficulty of information extraction from scanned documents represents a significant data processing challenge. From a research and innovation perspective, automatic text extraction of hospital documents enables innumerable possibilities such as improving diagnostics, clinical workflows and administrative processes. For example, AI methods can be applied to decades of untapped historical records to create prognostic models that cannot be developed in any other way.
Here, we present pyonb (https://github.com/SAFEHR-data/pyonb), an open-source Python SDK for automated document-to-text conversion, designed for clinical processing (although it is content-agnostic so useable for any text extraction task). pyonb bundles multiple open-source OCR tools (including Marker, Sparrow, PaddleOCR, and more) with a central forwarding API for requesting which OCR tool to execute. pyonb is designed as a suite of containerised services which can be deployed on a server to retrieve documents from a data warehouse for automated OCR and text extraction.
In this work we describe:
* the user requirements which motivated our design decisions * the software architecture * how developers can deploy the software and extend it to integrate their preferred OCR tool * the performance and processing speeds of a subset of OCR tools Acknowledgements This study was funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR, award code NIHR302495) and University College London Hospitals Biomedical Research Centre. The views expressed are those of the author(s) and not necessarily those of the NIHR or the Department of Health and Social Care. Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes Attendees will learn about the software engineering process and practicalities of creating a Python SDK for use in a hospital context, primarily for research purposes. They will benefit from learning about an array of open-source OCR tools, including assessment of how they perform, which may be applicable to their own work. They will learn how they might incorporate such freely available tools into their work or institution. Prerequisites The authors have a background in platform development and software engineering within healthcare institutions, so this work is directly applicable to attendees interested in building and deploying hospital data pipelines. More broadly, the work is valuable for any attendees interested in automated text extraction and OCR methods. The problem addressed is relevant to anyone interested in reuse and untapping archival data held back by lack of technologies to convert documents to text, not just healthcare enthusiasts. For a technical appreciation of the work, attendees would benefit from (but not be precluded without) an understanding or interest in Python, Docker, APIs, Apache Airflow, OCR methods and large language models. The software is open-source, therefore accessible to attendees from all sectors. The concept of text extraction from documents in the context of innovating future research is accessible and explainable regardless of attendee background or expertise.

event.title: Deploying and Customising KerkoApp: a successful internship project
event.description:
Abstract Have you or members of your institution been looking for an easy way to present a searchable collection of resources? KerkoApp is an open-source Python-based web application that provides an easy to use, searchable and browsable interface for bibliographic records stored in the Zotero reference management system. It is being used at the University of York to present a catalogue of the research outputs of a 5-year multi-institution plasma project (TDoTP) and as a community-driven resource for collating datasets and tools for researchers focusing on the human voice (YorVoice Catalogue).
The initial deployment and customisation of KerkoApp at York was the first project undertaken by our current year in industry RSE intern. It gave them the opportunity to learn aspects of a wide range of languages and technologies including virtual machines, Docker, Puppet, Python, Flask, Jinja, CSS, nginx and LLMs. They also developed their interpersonal and presentational skills through working closely with researchers on the TDoTP project and presenting the catalogue at the project's final advisory panel meeting.
Poster attendees will find out more about KerkoApp and how it has been deployed and customised at York. Attendees will also learn about the experiences of an RSE intern and the benefits that employing an RSE intern brings to the intern, the RSE team and the wider institution. This project demonstrates the value and benefits of establishing RSE career pathways and promoting RSE skills development within the context of DRI. Acknowledgements The work was funded by the "Multiscale turbulent dynamics of tokamak plasmas" EPSRC funded project (EP/R034737/1) and the University of York Sparks project YorVoice. Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes Participants will gain an understanding of the features and functionality of KerkoApp and how it can be deployed and customised. They will also learn about the experiences of an RSE intern working in a central Research IT team. Prerequisites No specific prerequisites but a general familiarity with software and its deployment would be beneficial.

event.title: Carpentries Lesson on Intermediate Research Software Development
event.description:
Abstract The Intermediate Research Software Development Course is now at the beta stage in the Carpentries Incubator. Along the path of its maturity, many pilot sessions have been conducted, asynchronous contributions made, and lessons learned as a result. A brief summary of the current status of the course will be displayed, including topics like successful delivery styles that have been used, alternate tooling options such as the popular VS Code IDE, and recent changes to the course content on software design and architecture. As course maintainers, we are always looking for new contributors, so a primary aim of this poster is to raise awareness of the course and its current status. Consequently, we will attract more interest from the RSE community to build a wider platform of support and increase uptake. To facilitate this, we will signpost routes and resources that new contributors can use to get involved. Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes This is a general interest submission, so there will be something for all audience members. Beginner research software developers will gain some awareness of topics they can investigate and look to foster on the pathway to eventually taking the course. Intermediate research software developers can assess whether the course will be useful to their skill set and identify any possible gaps which the course could help fill. Expert research software developers can comment on the relevance of the topics and delivery style of the course, helping the maintainers to improve the course and therefore give back to the research software community. Prerequisites Basic awareness of the Carpentries and computing tools they teach will be helpful but not essential to engage with the poster. A beginner level of experience with computer programming will be necessary to meaningfully engage with the poster. Beginners to experts in all domains should have something to engage with because the skills here are broadly applicable across any research domain that requires computing.

event.title: gprMax + MPI: Large-scale open-source computational electrodynamics
event.description:
Abstract gprMax is an open-source software package for computational electrodynamics. Designed with a general electromagnetic solver engine, it has a set of core features developed for modelling Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) and can be used to model electromagnetic wave propagation in fields such as engineering, geophysics, archaeology, and medicine. gprMax is a Python codebase with performance-critical parts using Cython.
This poster showcases the impact of research software engineers on enabling scientific research. Before this project, gprMax simulations could run using a CPU solver parallelised using OpenMP or a GPU solver developed using the NVIDIA CUDA programming model. However, these solvers ran on a single CPU node or GPU, preventing the full utilisation of HPC systems and limiting models to those that fit in the memory of a single node. Our work dramatically increases the modelling capabilities of gprMax by adding a Message Passing Interface (MPI) domain decomposition to the CPU solver that divides models between multiple nodes/MPI tasks. This can reduce the time to results when running on a single node, but more importantly, enables researchers to scale the size and/or resolution of their electromagnetic simulations, allowing them to utilise HPC systems and explore new science.
Additional improvements of interest to the RSE community include a Python interface to support file formats for parallel I/O (VTKHDF), a new suite of regression tests built for HPC using the ReFrame framework, and work to create visualisations of the model geometry and resultant electromagnetic field to demonstrate the new functionality in an accessible way. Acknowledgements This work was funded under the embedded CSE programme of the ARCHER2 UK National Supercomputing Service (https://www.archer2.ac.uk). Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes Attendees will see an example of research software engineering enabling new scientific capabilities. Key takeaways will include our approach to regression testing to ensure correctness of our MPI implementation and to check for regressions in the existing functionality, as well as our experience creating visualisations for a broad scientific audience. Prerequisites Basic understanding of HPC systems and software engineering for scientific applications would be beneficial. Knowledge of domain decomposition using MPI is advantageous but not required. A high-level understanding of electromagnetic waves may be useful; however, a detailed understanding is not necessary.

event.title: rplaywright: Bridging Playwright to R for Reproducible Web Automation in Research
event.description:
Abstract Dynamic web content plays an important role in research, from accessing public dashboards to automating testing workflows. However, R users face challenges when working with JavaScript-heavy websites, as most available tools rely on static HTML scraping or browser automation approaches that can be difficult to integrate smoothly into R workflows.
To address these challenges, rplaywright (https://erikaris.github.io/rplaywright/) was developed to integrate the R environment with Microsoft’s Playwright, a browser automation framework used across multiple programming languages. The package enables automated interaction with Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit browsers, operating in either headless or visible modes. It supports tasks such as navigating web pages, scrolling through dynamically loaded content, completing online forms, and extracting information from sites that update dynamically. Features including automatic waiting for page components, handling of infinite scrolling, and reliable interaction with dynamic interfaces facilitate reproducible workflows for research involving web resources.
rplaywright facilitates the seamless integration of dynamic web content into R-based research workflows, supporting scalable and reproducible data collection from interactive web portals. The project originated as part of the rOpenSci Champions Program, emphasising open development and community-driven technical mentorship. The package is suitable for workflows involving interactive data portals, social media platforms, and dynamic dashboards, enabling researchers to programmatically navigate pages, interact with filters, and extract underlying data for analysis. This poster will present the architecture of rplaywright, highlight key design considerations, demonstrate integration with popular R packages for streamlined analysis, and explore how cross-language tools can extend R’s capabilities to enhance research outcomes. Acknowledgements This project was initiated through my participation in the rOpenSci Champions Program 2024 (https://ropensci.org/blog/2024/02/15/champions-program-champions-2024/). I thank the rOpenSci team for their guidance and feedback throughout the development process. No external funding was received for this work. Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes This poster will help attendees understand what rplaywright is, how it works, and why it matters for research workflows involving the web. By adapting Playwright for R, it enables users to handle dynamic sites more reliably, perform basic browser-based checks, and integrate results directly into data processing pipelines. The poster will also share how combining R with tools from other languages can open up new possibilities for research software, and encourage attendees to collaborate on or adapt similar solutions. A GitHub link will be shared for those interested in exploring or contributing. Prerequisites Basic working knowledge of R and a general awareness of how websites function will help attendees follow the examples. No deep technical expertise is required, and key concepts will be explained using accessible language and, where helpful, diagrams. The poster is aimed at a broad audience, and will be especially relevant to those interested in automation tooling or reproducibility in web data workflows.

event.title: Create impactful scientific visualisations from your laptop*! (* also requires access to HPC)
event.description:
Abstract BlenderRemoteRender (Brr) is a client-server tool for working with Blender, specifically in a research context. Blender is a free and powerful 3D design and rendering toolkit. Although it is used more and more by the research community for producing high quality scientific visualisations, its primarily target is 3D artists. One of the key workflow difference being that researchers, unlike 3D artists and studios, may not have access to powerful rendering hardware locally or render farms. They however usually have remote access to High Performance Computing (HPC) resources setup with a job scheduler. Brr allows researchers to work on their scenes and visualisations locally on a light client while seamlessly connecting to HPC resources and submitting jobs via their scheduler to render images and animations. Because animation rendering is an embarrassingly parallel problem - each frame being independent of each other - Brr maximises Blender's parallel performance by dynamically scheduling frames to single GPUs or single CPU nodes and working with multiple nodes. In practice, Brr is composed of a Blender addon on the client side and a Zero MQ server both implemented in Python. The server is tasked with receiving configuration and data files from the client, submitting jobs to a queue system (like slurm) and sending back progress status and rendered images. Acknowledgements Funding by EPCC, University of Edinburgh. Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes The tool being presented is freely available and opensource (GPL license), attendees working with scientific data could directly benefit from knowing about the tool. The poster will also showcase examples of scientific visualisations made using Blender, attendees will get to see the capabilities and benefit that such software offer compared to tools more traditionally used in scientific contexts. Prerequisites In order to fully gasp the usefullness of the tool, some understanding of HPC workflow could be helpful. The audience isn't required to be familiar with Blender rendering nor with visualisation tools in general.

event.title: CATS: Climate-Aware Task Scheduler for environmentally conscious developers
event.description:
Abstract The Climate-Aware Task Scheduler is a lightweight Python package designed to schedule tasks based on the estimated carbon intensity of the electricity grid at any given moment. This tool uses real-time carbon intensity data from the UK's National Grid ESO via their API to estimate the carbon intensity of the electricity grid, and schedules tasks at times when the estimated carbon intensity is lowest. This helps to reduce the carbon emissions associated with running computationally intensive tasks, making it an ideal solution for environmentally conscious developers. The source code can be found at https://github.com/GreenScheduler/cats. Acknowledgements We are grateful to the staff of the Software Sustainability Institute and the organisers of Collaborations Workshop 2023 (CW23), whose efforts allowed us to enjoy the process of beginning the development of CATS as part of the CW23 Hack Day, and to others who contributed to the development via bug reports, questions, and the other contributions that help open-source software evolve. The author list is in alphabetical order. This work has been supported by the Software Sustainability Institute EPSRC, BBSRC, ESRC, NERC, AHRC, STFC and MRC (EP/S021779/1) and UKRI (AH/Z000114/1) grants. Authors
Event Type Poster Outcomes They will learn how they can use CATS to find the most environmentally sustainable time to run their HPC job. They will also learn how time of day and location influences computing carbon footprint. Prerequisites It requires some knowledge of running jobs on HPC, e.g. SLURM, but expert knowledge is not needed. No knowledge of sustainability is needed to understand the tool. The poster will make sure to introduce all the key concepts (e.g. both on the sustainability and HPC side) so that the concept and benefits of the tool can be grasp by the broad audience of RSEcon.

event.title: DataMap: A Scalable Microservices-Based Platform for Democratising and Analysing Massive Biological Knowledge Graphs
event.description:
Abstract Researchers across the UK Dementia Research Institute (UK DRI) generate hundreds of TB of data monthly, including genomics, proteomics, transcriptomics, behavioural, and neuroimaging data. Despite this vast output, much of the data remains siloed within individual labs, making it easy to share and collaborate on single datasets but difficult to integrate and collaborate on combined analyses across the institute and broader community. To address this, we developed DataMap—a network-based, interactive platform designed to democratise access to UK DRI’s heterogeneous research data by allowing researchers an easy and reliable mechanism for viewing and analysing their findings.
DataMap builds on a large-scale knowledge graph stored in Neo4j, integrating multimodal datasets and enabling researchers to query and explore complex biological relationships. However, querying such a massive and evolving graph is computationally intensive. To overcome this, we adopted a microservices-based architecture, supported by in-memory data structures and metaprogramming. This allows us to decouple memory-heavy operations, scale components independently, and adapt the platform to evolving user needs and new data types.
Here, we demonstrate how DataMap enables seamless and efficient interaction of UK DRI datasets via a user-centric web interface. Users can navigate biological entities, explore connections between data layers, and retrieve insights—all without requiring technical expertise. The system’s flexibility and scalability make it well-suited for the demands of dynamic research environments, allowing us to maximise knowledge extraction from our generated data. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery Hybrid (Both In-Person and Online Presenters) Outcomes Attendees will learn how to address the challenges of integrating, accessing, and visualising large-scale biological datasets using modern software engineering techniques. This session introduces DataMap, a scalable, microservices-based platform designed to democratise complex knowledge graphs for dementia research and beyond. Participants will see practical examples of using in-memory data structures and metaprogramming to solve latency, memory, and flexibility issues. The session is aimed at a broad audience, including researchers, engineers, and data scientists, and will demonstrate how non-technical users can interact intuitively with vast datasets. Attendees will leave with new strategies for building flexible, accessible data platforms to advance scientific research. Prerequisites Basic familiarity with software architectures, the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), databases and Python.

event.title: A Data Science Platform for the National Oceanography Centre and Beyond
event.description:
Abstract One of the common issues faced in the world of research software is "it worked on my machine". In this talk, we will present our efforts at the National Oceanography Centre (NOC) to solve this problem and make the task of writing shareable and reusable software easier by building an interactive Data Science Platform (DSP) based upon JupyterHub. The platform is accessed through a web browser and includes the Pangeo [https://pangeo.io/] stack along with popular machine learning libraries. In addition to a Jupyter notebooks interface we have integrated Matlab and a remote desktop service, removing the need for users to install these locally or rely on X forwarding/NoMachine/VNC.
The DSP was first deployed on servers owned by NOC. We are employing cloud native technologies such as Kubernetes and S3 style object stores as the basis for much of our digital research infrastructure. This allows us to deploy instances of the DSP on commercial cloud and national computing facilities, providing a uniform user experience regardless of the underlying system. Where the DSP’s server is not powerful enough, we use Dask to enable access to high performance computing or cloud computing resources.
In addition to providing a resource for developing and running research code, the platform is ideal for training. We use it regularly for Carpentries workshops since it provides all the software the learners require, resulting in a significant time saving during workshops, and allows ongoing access after the workshop.
As well as a demonstration of this platform, we will present our experiences of deploying and running it, including lessons we have learnt along the way and our plans for its future. Acknowledgements This work has been funded by the Natural Environment Research Council (NERC) projects Atlantic Climate and Environment Strategic Science (AtlantiS) and Climate Linked Atlantic Sector Science (CLASS). Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes We expect attendees to come away with an understanding of some of the common issues faced by an / our RSE team in a research institution and how we are attempting to solve multiple of these issues with one platform. We think presenting our Data Science Platform at RSECon would be useful to others in the community considering building comparable pieces of digital research infrastructure, as we’ll be sharing things we’ve learnt along the way, but we’d also like to discuss with and learn from others who have done similar. Prerequisites There are no prerequisites to learn from this talk. While it might be most of interest to those who already understand some of the issues RSEs face working on fast-paced research projects, these issues will be explained before we discuss the solution we’ve reached. Equally, the technical details of that solution will be explained without an assumption of prior knowledge.

event.title: Describing Data for Discovery: RSEs, Croissant, and the Future of Research Metadata
event.description:
Abstract Many research projects collect or create datasets as part of their outcomes, but these are often hard to find, interpret, or reuse. A key reason is the lack of structured, machine-readable metadata that can support both human understanding and automated tooling. This creates friction with data discovery, integration, and reuse—especially in machine-learning workflows.
This talk makes a case for adopting Croissant, a metadata format developed by MLCommons to address these challenges. It provides a standardised vocabulary and structure to describe datasets in ways that can be validated, shared, and used programmatically. Although Croissant originated from the ML community, its design is broadly applicable to any research data ecosystem. RSEs are in a unique position to help the widespread adoption of such standards. Since we often work with tools and platforms that manage datasets, we can embed good metadata practices by design, not as an afterthought.
The talk elaborates on what it looks like in practice to integrate Croissant into a real-world project workflow. To this end, we draw on EnergySHR, a project supporting AI for energy and sustainability. It aims to help researchers share energy-related datasets and references. During submission, users provide metadata to generate structured, machine-readable descriptions of each dataset. These are validated and embedded into the dataset's page. This helps support structured web search and enables automated loading of datasets in downstream workflows.
By embedding standards like Croissant into the tools we build and support, RSEs can make research outputs more visible and reusable. These are not just technical improvements but key contributions to research excellence. Acknowledgements This work is part of the EnergySHR project at TU Delft. I would like to thank Prof. Dr. M.M. de Weerdt, the project’s principal investigator, for introducing me to the Croissant metadata format and supporting its exploration within the project. I also acknowledge the MLCommons Croissant working group, whose active and responsive community has been instrumental in guiding implementation efforts. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes The audience will leave with an understanding of what Croissant is and why it is gaining traction. They’ll see how the standard can be applied in a practical context—without overhauling existing platforms. The talk will also highlight the role RSEs can play in shaping the adoption of emerging metadata standards and contributing to the long-term usability of research data. Prerequisites This talk is meant for anyone who works with data platforms, metadata standards, or research dataset workflows. A basic understanding of how datasets are shared, stored, or published will be helpful, but no deep domain knowledge is required. The concept of structured metadata will be introduced in accessible terms, and technical examples will be explained clearly, with minimal jargon. Attendees at any level—whether exploring metadata for the first time or working on mature data platforms—should find value in understanding how emerging standards like Croissant can be practically adopted.

event.title: Geoscience SIG Inaugural Meeting: sharing knowledge and building bridges across the geoscience community.
event.description:
Abstract Following the successful Weather and Climate Birds of a Feather session at RSECon24, the Geoscience Special Interest Group (SIG) was formed, with over 100 RSEs signed up to our slack space. The geoscience RSE community consists of many RSEs working across the various fields of geoscience, spanning, among others, climate, weather, space science, geology and oceanography.
In last year’s session, the needs and interests of this community were discussed. Those identified included a need for opportunities to share knowledge between organisations, break down silos and collaborate as well as interest in developing better guidance on career pathways.
As the inaugural hybrid meeting of the newly formed Geoscience SIG, we propose a BoF event to address these interests, aiming to build this community by bringing together RSEs from across the fields to network and facilitate knowledge exchange. This session is open to any RSEs working in or interested in geoscience and will feature keynotes from Bryan Lawrence (NCAS) & Andrea Sharpe (NERC), lightning talks on technical topics from within the community, breakout sessions to discuss community-driven topics (such as careers and building domain knowledge) and a session on the next steps for the SIG. Acknowledgements This BoF has had input from the wider RSE geoscience SIG committee beyond that of the author list, and any help given has been greatly appreciated. Additional information
Authors
Event Type Birds of a Feather In-Person or Online Delivery Hybrid (Both In-Person and Online Presenters) Outcomes We aim for this session to act as a technical knowledge exchange across subject disciplines as well as to strengthen ties within the community and share experiences (best practices/pitfalls) across different groups. We hope this session will also offer those interested in working in this area in the future an opportunity to find out more about what is involved and how they might find a job. As a tangible outcome, we aim to create a blog post from the session, highlighting the keynote, technical talk and summary. We also aim to use the breakout discussions as a basis for creating resources to add to the geoscience SIG website, e.g. starting points for those wanting to work in the area. After the session, participants will be able to expand their network and connections via new sign-ups to the SIG mailing list and Slack channel. Prerequisites This session is aimed at RSEs who are working in or are interested in the geosciences. event.title: Hands-on reproducible computing with Guix
event.description:
Abstract Effective computational research requires combination of programs, data and a runtime environment to produce new data to be analyzed and get results eventually published. Trust and value in open science rely on the ability to reproduce results published in the past literature, and to replicate or generalize the results of a study with new data in the future. Yet, a significant portion of studies cannot be reproduced, even by their very same authors [1].
Computational environments constitute a large source of analytical variability because they are insufficiently captured. With the large adoption of open source, software relies on an ever-growing list of dependencies, sometimes spanning multiple languages. Besides its complexity, the resulting dependency graph is under a constant flux of changes, with new releases, bug-fix and security updates. Such a complex and volatile graph cannot be captured by a simple README file [2].
Specialized tooling is required to efficiently formalize, build and deploy reproducible computational environments. Guix is a package manager, running on GNU/Linux, designed with such reproducibility in mind [3]. It can build and execute binaries independently from the host system, perform builds from source at any point in time, and deploy programs and environments to various targets, including containers.
This workshop provides a guided tour of Guix, focused on introducing the key concepts and commands of this tool, and getting hands-on experience with its practice. First, you will be introduced to the Guix package management commands, create a reproducible environment with `guix shell`, and deploy it with `guix time-machine`. Then, we will walk you through the process of Guixifying a representative scientific pipeline from the neuroimaging community [4]. The session will end with a discussion on Guix adoption in HPC, some of its advanced features, and available support channels.
[1] https://doi.org/10.1038/533452a
[2] https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-022-01720-9
[3] https://inria.hal.science/hal-01161771v2
[4] https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9 Additional information
Authors
Event Type Workshop In-Person or Online Delivery Hybrid (Both In-Person and Online Presenters) Outcomes (1) Understand the limitations of traditional package and environment managers, and how Guix addresses them. (2) Learn how to use Guix to reproduce experiments at a past or future timepoint. (3) Learn what tools are available to faciltate edition of Guix package recipes. (4) Distribute software in a reproducible way to both Guix and non-Guix users, as a standalone archive, container, or system package. Prerequisites Familiarity with GNU/Linux and using the command line is desirable. Experience with software packaging is a plus, but not strictly required.

event.title: Hands-on AIRR Workshop Using Dawn
Introducing Isambard-AI
The Promises and Perils of Trusted Research Environments
event.description:
Abstract Data Science and machine learning are powered by data, and there is plenty of data today: many human activities are powered by software that generates large quantities of it. While large datasets are constantly generated, putting them in the hands of the engineers and researchers, who can better exploit them, is not always easy. In domains like finance or health, data sensitivity and user privacy require a limited and controlled distribution of data assets.
Arguably, the gold standard for solving this data availability problem is placing datasets within trusted research environments (TREs). TREs are closed computational environments equipped with technical and process controls that enable secure data access to vetted researchers. The Research Engineering Team at the Turing uses a TRE software, our in-house developed Data Safe Haven, alongside our trusted research process to support academic projects of diverse sizes and domains.
We learned that while software and processes are pivotal to the success of a TRE initiative, there are other external critical factors that, if ignored, can derail an academic project. For example, placing data in a TRE comes with regulatory and legal obligations that need to be addressed way before onboarding the researchers into the system. Or dealing with researcher frustration when facing the necessary security controls imposed by platform and process. In this talk, we will rely on years of experience to describe these external factors, their influence on the success of a TRE initiative, and how we approach them at Turing.
We will discuss:
* Enabling data-driven research with TREs. * Software and process: The essential factors of every TRE initiative. * External critical factors: Legal, financial, data management, usability, and others. * The Turing way of dealing with these factors, to ensure a successful TRE initiative. Acknowledgements This work is supported by the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) Grant EP/Z531297/1. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery Hybrid (Both In-Person and Online Presenters) Outcomes After this talk participants will understand: 1) how TREs enable data accessibility in academic projects, 2) the software and process needed to put a TRE initiative in place, and 3) the external critical success factors of academic projects running on TREs, and how we approach them at the Turing. Prerequisites Our talk is of interest to researchers and engineers involved in academic projects that deal with sensitive data, either by using Trusted Research Environments or other data protection techniques. The topics we will discuss do not assume familiarity with sensitive data management or trusted research environment development.

event.title: Loome: Empowering research teams with scalable, secure cloud resources
event.description:
Abstract Public cloud offers a huge range of services to choose from, many of which can be valuable research tools. Choosing, deploying and using these tools can be complex and overwhelming. How can research teams be offered choice without unnecessary complexity, opening equitable access to cloud to all, regardless of your background and expertise.
This session will provide a walkthrough of the Loome platform from a research team’s perspective, a cloud management layer implemented in Microsoft Azure to abstract unnecessary complexities away from research end-users whilst providing governance and control for IT teams. Authors

event.title: Transforming Digital Research Infrastructure for Environmental Science
event.description:
Abstract Delivering cutting-edge Digital Research Infrastructure (DRI) to support environmental science demands more than just new tools—it requires a fundamental shift in how we work. Much like the proverb “It takes a village to raise a child,” delivering effective DRI demands contributions from a broad community of professionals. Success depends not only on Research Software Engineering (RSE), but also on the combined efforts of experts in DevOps, data science, data management, and design (including Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and Software Architecture) .
At UKCEH, we’ve embraced a multidimensional approach, drawing on this diverse range of skills and practices. Our large, multi-year DRI projects integrate methodologies such as Agile (Scrum and Kanban), PRINCE2, and co-design. This mix isn't always seamless. We share how these varied approaches and skill sets intersect in practice—what’s worked, where friction has arisen, and how we've adapted to meet the evolving demands of digital environmental science. Acknowledgements Gordon Blair (UKCEH), Kelly Widdocks (UKCEH) Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Attendees will gain an understanding of how we approach delivering DRI at UKCEH and which process we have found work. Prerequisites Aim is for this to be accessible for all. No prior knowledge needed. More suited to RSE leaders, but aimed at all.

event.title: Towards Cloud-Native Workflows for Environmental Data: Lessons from NOC and UKCEH
event.description:
Abstract Scientific datasets are continuing to increase in size. Traditional methods of data analysis are struggling with the increased local storage and compute resources required. As a result, a transition to cloud-based technologies and ways of working is becoming increasingly necessary. This talk shares the ongoing collaboration between the UK’s National Oceanography Centre (NOC) and the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology (UKCEH) to explore management, sharing and analysis of large gridded environmental datasets based in the cloud. Our goal is to make the transition to working with datasets on the cloud as easy as possible for researchers.
We will focus on three key areas: object storage: what it is and why we are using it, cloud-native data formats and how we convert between them at scale, and interfaces for visualising and working with the data.
We store our data in object storage systems using Zarr and Kerchunk formats, which support massively-parallel access over the web and thus scalable computations. We’ve tested different ways to convert data, and will share what works well and what doesn’t.
Using these formats come with its own set of challenges however. Key amongst these is the requirement that data is split into chunks. Chunk size strongly influences speed of data processing and visualisation but chunk sizes that are good for scientific analysis are not good for visualisation. We will share how we have attempted to mitigate this and other related challenges.
We’ll show benchmarks comparing different methods and chunking strategy performance on the data conversion, simple scientific analyses and the tile-server visualisation, and share successes, challenges and tips that folk can take away from our work so far. We hope it will help others who are thinking about or working towards making their data systems more cloud-ready. Acknowledgements At UKCEH, this work has been supported by the Flood and Drought Research Infrastructure (FDRI) project, funded by a capital award from the Natural Environment Research Council (NERC). At NOC, support was provided by the Atlantic Climate and Environment Strategic Science (AtlantiS) programme, also funded by NERC. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes This talk will provide key insights into the challenges of transitioning to a cloud-native data analysis workflow, along with practical starting points for mitigation—such as optimal strategies for data conversion and a blueprint for a workflow that enables interactive visualisation. All code that is mentioned will be made available through GitHub via links and QR codes at the end of the presentation. We will also highlight the benefits of working together across different organisations! Prerequisites This talk is aimed at people who work with large datasets, especially geospatial data. It will be helpful to have some basic knowledge of formats like NetCDF and experience with tools such as xarray. A general understanding of cloud concepts—like object storage, parallel processing, or web maps that use tiles—will also make the content easier to follow. That said, we’ll explain the key ideas clearly, so those without a technical background will be able to follow the discussion too.

event.title: Fluid: Towards Transparent, Explorable Research Outputs
event.description:
Abstract Although open science principles like FAIR data aim to make scientific results more accessible, intelligible and reusable, in practice “open” usually just means that data sets and source code are available for download. The charts, figures and text used to present scientific claims remain difficult to interpret or challenge, even for experts. What can we do to build on today's baseline of best practices to address these more ergonomic needs?
Fluid is a new programming language designed to support transparent visualisation and reporting for web-based documents. Fluid provides a runtime environment with built-in tracking of fine-grained data dependencies; this allows us to integrate data lineage information -- views of the relevant underlying data -- directly into charts and figures, through additional interactions. Selecting a graphical element in a chart can automatically reveal the relevant data, and highlight elements in other visualisations that use the same data.
This presentation will introduce Fluid's syntax and execution model, demonstrate the current tooling, and report on a user study exploring the impact of transparent visualisations on interpretability and trust. We will also demonstrate how to incorporate lineage queries into textual content. For example, if a paragraph of a climate report claims that under a particular emissions scenario, global warming of 2°C is “extremely likely” to be exceeded in the 20th century, a researcher can use Fluid to link key fragments of text to the underlying data and queries over those data sets, so that someone interested in exploring the evidence base can drill into the underlying data without leaving the context of the report.
The session will be relevant to data scientists and research software engineers interested in how software infrastructure might help support the ergonomic goals of open science, at least for web-based documents. More information and interactive examples are available at https://f.luid.org. Authors
Event Type Walkthrough In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes The audience will gain an insight into how developments in programming languages and runtime environments might support FAIR values like transparency, accessibility and interpretability, complementing existing open science practices that are (thankfully) increasingly widespread. This is a relatively unexplored topic; we hope to convince the audience that it is a worthwhile direction, using examples framed around _explorable explanations_ (interactive essays designed to communicate challenging technical ideas) and _transparent charts and reports_ (climate and other reports that integrate the evidence base directly into a document). We also hope to highlight some of the difficulties in making this sort of infrastructure more mainstream, and supporting the flexibility and customisation needs of different user communities. Overall, we would like the audience to come away with the sense that this is an exciting new direction, that also opens up several challenging (meta-)research questions. Prerequisites This session will be of potentially broad interest, given the overall topic of tooling and infrastructure for open science. Some parts of the walkthrough will present Fluid code; some familiarity with functional programming (list comprehensions, lambdas, map/reduce-like operations, and data structures like records and lists) will be useful.

event.title: From Research Prototype to Real-World Impact with Nuvolos: Reproducibility and Collaboration at Scale
event.description:
Abstract RSEs work at the intersection of research and software engineering, combining domain expertise with technical skill to deliver reproducible science. But too much of that time is swallowed by fixing broken dependencies, rebuilding environments for each project, and keeping infrastructure running. Nuvolos takes on the heavy computational lifting, provisioning, scaling, and managing compute, so RSEs can focus on the science itself.
Nuvolos is a seamlessly integrated, powerful, and collaborative cloud‑based computational workspace. It removes operational friction, simplifies software setup, and ensures computational environments are instantly available, anywhere, through a browser.
Designed with the evolving needs of the RSE community in mind, Nuvolos reflects shared values that drive sustainable, high‑impact research:
* Empowerment – Instant access to tools like Python, R, Julia, MATLAB, Stata, any IDE, backed by scalable CPU & GPU compute. * Reproducibility & Rigor – Full versioning ensures every experiment can be trusted, verified, and built upon. * Collaboration & Accessibility – Seamless teamwork across institutions with shared, browser‑based access to computational resources. * Sustainability & Reusability – Maintainable code, reusable workflows, and preserved datasets extend research impact beyond a single project. * Community Contribution – Support for open science practices, helping RSEs share tools, methods, and results with the wider community. * Innovation & Agility – Continuous integration of the latest frameworks, from TensorFlow and PyTorch to AlphaFold, keeps research on the cutting edge. * Simplicity & Control – Backend complexity is managed for you, while you retain full control over projects and environments.
Nuvolos is more than a platform. It is a partner in advancing science that is sustainable, reproducible, and openly shared, helping the RSE community work more productively, collaboratively, and with lasting impact. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Following this talk you will learn about the Nuvolos platform how it encourages collaboration and reproducibility in research. Prerequisites N.A.

event.title: Bridging Academia and Industry: An RSE’s Perspective on Commercial Collaboration
event.description:
Abstract Research Software Engineers (RSEs) often operate at the intersection of software development and academic inquiry. However, their roles can extend far beyond traditional research boundaries. This presentation explores the unique challenges and insights gained from working as an RSE on a commercial project in partnership with a university. Unlike typical research-focused roles, commercial engagements involve navigating complex contract negotiations, company politics, and differing expectations in project management and delivery. Drawing from a recent experience, I will detail a collaboration where a company initially relied on generative AI to convert mathematical formulas into Python code. When the results fell short, both mathematical insight and computational rigor were needed—prompting the company to seek support from our university. This case study highlights the technical, organizational, and interpersonal skills required of RSEs in commercial settings, as well as the pros and cons of stepping beyond purely research-oriented work. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Attendees will gain a practical understanding of the differences between academic and commercial project work from an RSE perspective. They will learn about the challenges involved in setting up and delivering a university-industry collaboration, including legal, organizational, and communication hurdles. Through a real-world case study, attendees will see how technical and domain expertise can add value where AI-generated solutions fall short. The talk will highlight the skills RSEs need to operate effectively in commercial contexts and help attendees reflect on how such opportunities can expand their role beyond traditional research. Attendees will leave with insights into the pros and cons of engaging with industry and actionable considerations for future commercial partnerships. Prerequisites This talk is intended for Research Software Engineers, software developers in academia, and research project managers with an interest in industry collaboration. Attendees should have a basic understanding of the RSE role and experience working in or alongside academic research environments. Familiarity with software development practices (especially in Python) and the general research project lifecycle will be beneficial. No prior experience with commercial projects is required, but attendees should be open to exploring the operational and cultural differences between academic and industry collaborations. Some exposure to AI-generated code or mathematical computing may help contextualize the case study but is not essential.

event.title: Making a SPLASH: How digital tools are revolutionising wave overtopping prediction
event.description:
Abstract The SPLASH project has created an environmental digital twin able to forecast and visualise wave overtopping to support coastal communities in high-risk flooding areas. It provides an excellent example of RSE teams combining user centred design, interactive plotting, machine learning and containerisation to take a scientist’s proof of concept Jupyter notebook to an easy-to-use web dashboard.
The SPLASH digital twin uses a random forest machine learning model trained on wind, water level and wave data combined with wave overtopping data from a WireWall sensor. A test scenario is based around the coastal railway in Dawlish, Devon, and a coastal frontage with high social value (recreation and tourism) in Penzance, Cornwall. Overtopping data and forecast conditions are displayed on an interactive dashboard able to display wave overtopping graphs from today up to five days ahead. This dashboard also allows users to adjust the wave, water level and atmospheric features to predict new overtopping scenarios and understand how these variables influence the overtopping hazard. The tool is built using a Plotly Dash frontend and models in scikit-learn. Up-to-date wave and wind forecast data is obtained from the Met Office through a set cron scripts and the tidal levels are obtained from local predictions. A set of Docker containers are used to run the frontend, backend and downloader making the whole system easy to deploy on a dedicated server, virtual machine or cloud provider. This research shows how integrating machine learning models with digital technologies enables prediction of wave overtopping very efficiently. This digital tool serves as a decision-support system for mitigating coastal hazard, e.g. impact by overtopping waves, benefiting both community policy makers and railway operators with infrastructure in affected regions. Acknowledgements This research was funded by the Natural Environment Research Council (NERC) and the Met Office through their TWINE programme of which the SPLASH project (NE/Z503423/1 and NE/Z503435/1)was part. The digital twin was trained using data collected by the NERC funded CreamT project (NE/V002538/1). Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery Hybrid (Both In-Person and Online Presenters) Outcomes 1. How to build a tool to predict wave overtopping events. 2. How to leverage user centric design to build a highly usable and accessible dashboard. 3. How to leverage machine learning models with wave and atmospheric variables, and digital technologies to build an application able to forecast wave overtopping timely and reliably. 4. How to leverage containerisation to combine all the above into a package that can be easily deployed on any hosting platform. Prerequisites Someone interested in basic software engineering and how to combine digital technologies like Plotly Dash with Machine Learning models.

event.title: bead: A Data Provenance Tool for Diverse Teams
event.description:
Abstract Reproducing research results requires knowing exactly which version of the data was used and understanding the steps taken to clean and analyse it. This can be challenging in distributed environments with many contributors.
bead (https://bead.zip) is a simple command-line tool and archive format that systematically documents data workflows. Each saved "bead" captures a single processing step: the input data (via unique references), the code used, and the resulting outputs—whether cleaned datasets, visualisations, or reports. By recording these steps and linking them via input references, bead facilitates easy review, maintenance, and re-execution of computations, while also fostering collaboration.
This talk will begin by introducing the problem, followed by a demo/presentation of the tool, and will conclude with a discussion of its long-term application in Economics research at Central European University. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Attendees will understand the problem of reproducible research computing, and will have enough understanding and information to use the tool to create computational chains. Prerequisites bead is a command-line tool, so some familiarity with Unix, Mac or Windows shells is necessary. Otherwise, bead is tool agnostic: your code may be in Python, R, SQL or any other language capable of reading and writing files.

event.title: PAIDIVERPY: An Open-Source Python package designed to create pipelines for preprocessing image data for biodiversity analysis.
event.description:
Abstract Biologists and ecologists are increasingly using imaging systems to study the natural world. Getting meaningful biodiversity metrics from visual data requires reliable, reproducible image preprocessing. However, existing tools for image preprocessing are fragmented, application-specific, not well documented, and not designed for the needs of ecologists. This lack of standardization makes reproducibility difficult and slows down scientific progress. To address these challenges, we present PAIDIVERPY—an open-source modular Python package designed to simplify, standardize, and document image preprocessing workflows for biodiversity analysis.
PAIDIVERPY is a flexible framework for building reproducible image preprocessing pipelines, complete with detailed documentation, and traceability for each step and image. The package is designed in collaboration with ecologists, enabling them to create and visualise preprocessing workflows without deep technical expertise. Users can easily add, remove, and customize steps, preview results at every stage, and output fully documented workflows in a standardized format.
The tool supports preprocessing of complex biodiversity image datasets collected from diverse instruments and deployment strategies. Users can apply pixel-level transformations such as colour correction and backscatter removal, and subsample data to ensure unbiased metric estimation. The software also enables integration of custom algorithms alongside built-in processing steps, enhancing flexibility. To accommodate large datasets, PAIDIVERPY includes built-in support for parallelization using Dask and integration with batch schedulers for HPC environments. Its configuration system allows users to define processing steps in a structured, interoperable format, promoting reproducibility and simplifying modifications.
Extensive tutorials and documentation accompany the tool. Additionally, two curated image sets from plankton and benthic surveys, complete with metadata, are provided to support testing and exploration.
PAIDIVERPY enables ecologists to focus on scientific analysis while reducing the technical burden of data preparation. It bridges the gap between ecological expertise and AI-powered image analysis by making image preprocessing accessible, efficient, and reproducible. Acknowledgements This project was supported by the UK Natural Environment Research Council (NERC) through the Tools for automating image analysis for biodiversity monitoring (AIAB) Funding Opportunity, reference code UKRI052. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Attendees will learn how the PAIDIVERPY software was built to make image preprocessing easier for scientists. The presentation will show how different parts of the tool—like image filters, metadata support, and processing steps—were designed to work together in a flexible and reusable way. It will cover key features such as pipeline visualization, saving and tracking changes, and using configuration files to set up workflows. Attendees will also see how the software runs faster on large datasets by using Dask and Slurm, and how users can add their own processing steps. The session will share practical tips on building open-source tools that are easy to use, adaptable, and reliable, especially for non-technical users. Prerequisites Basic python experience and some interest in image processing and computer vision.

event.title: The power of recognition: what RSEs can teach the research sector.
event.description:
Abstract Simon Hettrick is Director of Strategy at the Software Sustainability Institute and a Director of the Southampton Research Software Group. A pioneer of the Research Software Engineer (RSE) movement, he devised the campaign that grew the RSE community from a handful of people in 2013 to a worldwide community in the present day. He was the first Chair of the UK RSE Association and a founding trustee of the Society of Research Software Engineering. Simon used his experience with RSEs to create the Hidden REF: a campaign to recognise every output and every role that makes research possible. Authors

They are delivered by a prominent expert who can provide big-picture insights and inspire the audience. In-Person or Online Delivery Prerequisites None

event.title: Emerging voices
"Where do the people come from?"—A mixed methods investigation of Research Software Engineering
event.description:
Abstract Over the last decade, the idea of a role of Research Software Engineer (rse) has gained some adoption. The RSE is a skilled software engineer who focuses on the construction of software for use in research. In a brief time, the idea has gone from a defining term created at a workshop on software sustainability to a job title and group name used at numerous research institutions worldwide, with member societies sharing experience and advocating for career recognition. In short, we are witnessing the creation of a new profession of Research Software Engineering.
In April 2025, the presenter defended their doctoral thesis, in which we described their design and implementation of a mixed-methods investigation (containing both quantitative and qualitative components) into the development and propagation of RSE, drawing on relevant theories from the sociology of professions. We believe this to be the first such systematic, scholarly investigation into RSE.
We implemented one quantitative and three qualitative studies of RSE, addressing questions on: the state of software engineering knowledge in research; the state of RSE as a profession; the independence of RSE from existing research practice; and the connection between the relationship of researchers and RSEs, and research software practice. Combining these studies into a single mixed-methods programme, we create an overall picture of the state of RSE one decade into its inception, and an evidence-based “manifesto” for future change in the field. We present our research into RSE, our findings, and our recommendations from the manifesto. Acknowledgements The work was supported by a Progress Scholarship from Kellogg College, Oxford. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Attendees will discover the current status of RSE as a field based on gathering data of multiple kinds, in addition to evidence-based recommendations for moving the field forward. These recommendations are relevant to RSEs, RSE leaders, funders, and employers. Prerequisites This talk doesn't have any technical prerequisites. Anyone interested in the development of RSE as a career or discipline can attend this talk.

event.title: Towards a National Research Software Engineering Capability: evidencing the impact of RSEs
event.description:
Abstract We present an exciting new co-authored Roadmap outlining how to establish a national, people-centred Arts & Humanities (A&H) RSE Capability. Underpinned by a new evidence bank demonstrating the impact RSEs make on research, this work, though focused on one domain, has relevance across the research landscape.
We reflect on the process of creating these outputs, including the careful community management and design that motivated a stakeholder group of 40 co-authors. We also address how we responded to an unexpected but vital funder question: ‘Where is the evidence that RSEs are worth investing in?’ The evidence bank provides a compelling answer, detailing how RSEs organise, interpret, and find meaning in vast and complex data, enabling outputs, accelerating research, and even reducing costs.
The Roadmap acknowledges that infrastructure is both technical and social. Designed with a community of leaders and potential users, it responds to the need to avoid duplication by connecting and extending existing infrastructure. While rooted in A&H needs and challenges, it engages with the broader ecosystem, aiming for integration between domains rather than further separation. It is grounded in case studies that evidence existing impactful RSE capability models across A&H, cultural heritage, and social sciences and that highlight both the potential and need to scale: in terms of user communities, good practice, and innovation pathways. Crucially, the Roadmap also proposes a metascientific research effort to inform strategy, evaluate impact, and support the sector in adapting to evolving technologies and policies. All of this supports open scholarship practices to maximise impact, engagement, and value for money.
