event.title: From Lab to Launch: The evolving role of RSEs in driving sustainable and commercially viable digital solutions
event.description:
Abstract Research Software Engineers (RSEs) have championed software development best practices and infrastructure standards to enable more reusable, sustainable and reproducible research tools. Their role continues to evolve, with these tools now driving societal impact through commercial and digital solutions. Today, RSEs, supported by Research Data Stewards (RDSs), provide both technical expertise including system design, data governance, quality assurance, and project management; and essential soft skills that underpin sustainable digital infrastructure. At University College London’s Centre for Digital Innovation (CDI) and Advanced Research Computing Centre (ARC), we see the growing need to broaden RSEs’ expertise to develop digital products that serve the public good and support commercially viable ventures. This shift involves understanding areas beyond coding, such as intellectual property, business model design, open-source innovation, data security, and technical leadership. In this talk, we will showcase how RSEs and RDSs are driving mission-led, globally focused solutions. We will also share real-world use cases and discuss the challenges in translating research into meaningful societal impact. We will cover: (1) Overview of UCL CDI Impact Accelerator programme, (2) Research commercialisation landscape and translational research, (3) Difficulties that university spin-outs face compared to startups, (4) Role of RSE in technical support of academic entrepreneurs, (5) Overview of typical problems with producing research code and building product teams. We will conclude with a call to action to join our community of RSEs driving commercially viable solutions and invite everyone to explore and contribute to our workshop materials, available on our GitHub: CDI-Hub. Acknowledgements We would like to thank our colleagues at AWS, whose industry experience is helping to drive forward products with a greater chance of making real impact. We acknowledge the support of the Advanced Research Computing Centre in developing new skills for Research Software Engineers (RSEs), by backing teams that are working to take research through to production. We thank UCL for their funding, provided through the capital IT investment portfolio. Additional information If we decide to publish the materials, we will check with the organisers first to confirm which content can be released under the Creative Commons Attribution Licence. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery Hybrid (Both In-Person and Online Presenters) Outcomes Participants will gain understanding of the current landscape of research commercialisation, including the processes and strategies for translating research into marketable products. They will also learn about the crucial role of RSEs in providing technical support to academic entrepreneurs, covering system design, data governance, and project management. Additionally, attendees will understand how RSEs and RDSs contribute to creating impactful, commercially viable digital solutions, along with practical insights and strategies for overcoming common challenges in this field. Prerequisites This talk is aimed at Research Software Engineers and Research Data Stewards of all levels, from beginners to experts, who are interested in developing commercially viable solutions.

event.title: How to build a project team: experiences from the Turing
event.description:
Abstract Research Software Engineers can be asked to work on a very wide range of projects. These project vary in many different ways, such as the number of people involved, the duration, whether they are fully internal to an organisation or working with external partners, or how much they are shaped by the RSEs. The requirements for RSEs can vary significantly too, meaning that identifying the optimum team for any given project can be challenging.
The Research Engineering Group at the Alan Turing Institute has approximately 40 people with a range of different skills (RSEs, Research Data Scientists, Research Computer Engineers, Data Wranglers). As a team we provide software engineering expertise to many of the projects that the Turing is working on. Over the past 5 years, there have been several changes in how we work. The team has grown significantly in size, and the Turing has gone through a transition from most projects being stand-alone to a mission based vision with a stronger focus on effective real-world impact. In the earlier phase, REG members would typically work on a couple of projects at a time, and they would change at least one of these projects relatively frequently. Under the new setup, team members typically only work on one mission at a time, often for much longer time periods.
This transition has created many opportunities, but also some challenges in how we work both as a team and individually. In this talk, we consider some of the lessons learned from this transition, and how they can be applied to RSE teams more generally when staffing projects. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Attendees will get benefit from the experience gathered by the ATI RSE team around project team building. Prerequisites No prerequisites are necessary

event.title: Let's stop pretending to be unicorns!
event.description:
Abstract Research software engineers as unicorns: Here comes the magical RSEcorn, flying in, solving all your problems!
Or does it?
The narrative of the omnipotent RSE which can be used "plug&play" in research projects might be useful for lobbying for recognition and funding, but is problematic for working relationships with researchers. Not only can it lead to frustrations on both sides, it is also the perfect ingredient for imposter syndrome for the RSE.
This talk is questioning the way that we, as the RSE community, tend to view and present ourselves, and how this develops into an unhealthy "us vs. them" culture in some parts of the community.
I also want to highlight where alternative collaboration patterns already exist, and propose an alternative image for ourselves within the wider research community. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes The talk is intended to spark discussions and thought processes about the RSE community and our interaction with the wider research community. I don't want to take away the unicorn as the RSE mascot! Prerequisites I hope that this talk will be accessible and interesting to a large fraction of the RSE community. No previous knowledge is needed, and I will very briefly give the historical context of the origins of the RSE community, for those who are not familiar with it.

event.title: Aligning feasible technical requirements to research objectives and steering collaboration: role and responsibilities of the Research Software Analyst in RSE teams
event.description:
Abstract This talk will focus on the role institutionalised at King’s Digital Lab of the Research Software Analyst as key member of the RSE team acting as first point of contact with project partners throughout a project / product lifecycle from collaborative requirements definition (including contribution to funding applications) to project management during evolutionary development (including negotiations around prioritisation of requirements / increments), testing of the solution components and negotiations around acceptance at release phase, to reporting and decommissioning at post-project phase.
The competences of this role are relevant for RSEs typically involved in complex research projects which require at minimum an agreed understanding of technical requirements with at least one other individual (e.g. project lead, other researcher / RSE / colleague, funder / sponsor, project partner). The role is particularly relevant for RSE groups and team operating at scale, delivering on complex projects with multiple stakeholders, running in parallel and often requiring concept design if not a full funding application with estimate of effort prior to starting.
Building on Agile DSDM roles definitions (https://www.agilebusiness.org/dsdm-project-framework/roles-and-responsibilities.html) and business analysis good practices, the role has evolved based on the specificity of the institutional context and research domains (mainly arts, humanities and social sciences) within which KDL operates; however, the talk will generalise the role profile and functions to enable the audience to identify potential alignment with other contexts and roles across disciplines.
The talk will focus on:
* RSA role description (standard, senior and principal levels) building on the document authored by KDL founding Director; * walkthrough project feasibility assessment phase aligned with research objectives and to inform funding applications with associated example/s compliant with KDL project templates; * outline of the activities led by the RSA during evolutionary development to monitor progress, steer collaboration with a variety of stakeholders and facilitate the solution development team work. Acknowledgements The KDL roles definition document was authored by KDL Founding Director James Smithies in 2019. Others in KDL as well as College, Faculty and wider community contributed to its review and refinements. In particular, KDL Principal RSE Miguel Vieira, RS project manager Alessandra Esposito and Senior RS bab manager Pam Mellen should be acknowledged for their input to the role’s evolution. Additional information I am unsure at this moment in time whether, if the talk is accepted, other authors will present and whether they will be all in person. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes The audience will gain knowledge of the role and responsibilities for an RSA in a modular format, so as to pick and choose what might be relevant for their context of work. In addition, they will gain insights into specific techniques used at feasibility assessment phase (what elements are considered for a project to be considered viable for an RSE team and how is this process led?) as well as suitable workflows to enable collaboration with diverse stakeholders often with conflicting priorities when a project is active. Pointers will be provided to further resources for those interested to go more in depth (e.g. around the decommissioning process). Prerequisites No specific skills or knowledge are expected to make sense of the talk; however, familiarity with the phases of Software Development Lifecycle and Agile frameworks of project and solution development are useful to contextualise some terminology around the RSA role and its functions. While the role is set within an HEI context, it aligns to business analysis practices and would be useful to audiences in academia as well as industry and other organisations undertaking stakeholder analysis, strategy and business cases related to technical design and development and more in general any research and development work.

event.title: ConveRSE - Let's Talk About Mental Health
event.description:
Abstract As part of my Software Sustainability Institute (SSI) Fellowship, I’ve been looking for ways to support mental health in the research software community. 1 in 4 adults experience mental health problems each year, and in 2022, Dave Horsfall conducted a survey which showed that a range of issues are common among Research Software Engineers (RSEs). This is hardly surprising, as working as an RSE or Research Technical Professional (RTP) presents a unique set of challenges; we have to deal with context and technology switching, impostor syndrome, limited career opportunities and recognition, on top of software development being notorious for burnout and… well, everything going on in the world right now! If not properly managed, it can be a recipe for mental health disaster, as I know only too well!
In this talk, I will tell the story of how I became a father in lockdown, how it led to burnout and an anxiety attack, and how that experience motivated me to apply for the Fellowship. I will explain why I believe it is essential to continue the conversation around mental health, to create an environment where people can discuss mental health in the workplace, and why it’s better to address issues before they turn into larger problems. I will look at what we can practically do to support mental health among RSEs (and those in similar professions), including some advice, best practices and other things I’ve learned from telling my story and discussing mental health at various events over the last couple of years. Finally, I will introduce ConveRSE - a new online hub for mental health information, projects and resources aimed at RSEs and RTPs - and encourage people to get involved so we can work together to create a better future for ourselves and our colleagues. Acknowledgements This work has been supported by the Software Sustainability Institute as part of their Fellowship Programme. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes I hope that the audience will come away with a greater understanding of mental health problems, how they can affect us all and why it is important to continue to break down stigmas and be more open about mental health in the workplace. Prerequisites No prerequisite skills or knowledge are required. I (will) have performed this talk to a variety of audiences, including RSEs, academics, PhD students etc., and have designed it to be as accessible to as wide an audience as possible.

event.title: What support does research software need? Early lessons from the Research Software Maintenance Fund
event.description:
Abstract Software is pervasive in modern research, used in every discipline and underpins many approaches including modelling and simulation; data management, analysis and visualisation; and experiment and laboratory control. Yet it can be difficult, even for widely used research software, to find resources for its maintenance, refactoring and community development, because the focus of much research funding is on novelty.
The Software Sustainability Institute is running the Research Software Maintenance Fund (RSMF), supported by the UKRI Digital Research Infrastructure programme, offering £4.8 million to support and sustain key research software, ensuring it remains reliable and accessible. This initiative is not only funding vital pieces of the research ecosystem but helps us understand what support research software needs to reduce technical debt and grow engagement and how we can effectively provide it.
In this short presentation, we’ll be presenting some early analysis of the types of activities that are being requested, putting them into the context of other research software funding initiatives, providing information on how the RSMF is operated, and getting feedback on what the community thinks is important to address next. Acknowledgements The Research Software Maintenance Fund is supported by funding from the UKRI Digital Research Infrastructure programme through grant AH/Z000114/1. We would like to thank all the SSI team members and advisory board members who provided input into the development of the RSMF. We also acknowledge the input we have received from the CZI EOSS programme team, in particular Kate Hertweck, and the ReSA Funders Forum. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Attendees will gain a general understanding of the current research software funding landscape, and a specific understanding of types of activities that the Research Software Maintenance Fund is being asked to support. They may also gain insight into how to apply for funding to maintain software. We expect this presentation to be of interest to anyone who is associated with a research software project in any role. No prior knowledge or experience of applying for funding, or the Research Software Maintenance Fund, is required. Prerequisites This presentation does not require any prerequisite skills or knowledge. Attendees may benefit from having experience of being involved in research software projects, particularly if they have been involved in the process of planning for future releases or community development.

event.title: An overview of the DisCouRSE Network+ grant: Developing a Community of Leaders in RSE and related professions
event.description:
Abstract I will introduce our newly funded UKRI Network+ grant, covering what we're aiming to accomplish in the next three years, and how we would like the whole community to get involved!
Scaling and sustaining the impact of digital Research Technical Professional (dRTP) communities like ours requires developing leaders who have an amplifying effect. Our central premise is to build from the critical mass of the UK RSE community, connecting and training cohorts of leaders, who can use our flexible fund to advance the skills and careers of all digital RTPs (not just RSEs). Much work has already been done, but opportunities are varied across role types and locations. Most success has been achieved through related professions working together, not by treating RSEs as a special case. We therefore seek to identify and expand such best practice, build stronger connections between those facing similar challenges, across sectors, and thereby make greater impact more rapidly. We are also investing in developing the Digital Research Competencies Framework to inform what training is needed for leaders, and partnering with existing experts to develop and deliver this at scale.
This talk will give a brief overview of the project and launch our first flexible funding call for proposals. We will distribute £1,000,000 as seed funding in multiple rounds over the next 3 years. I will describe the types of submission we are looking for (e.g. pilot projects, workshop series, training programmes, and the like) and how to apply for funding.
Related sessions with more interaction include 123, 127, and the training satellite day on Friday. Acknowledgements This project has received funding through the UKRI Digital Research Infrastructure Programme under grant reference UKRI737. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes All attendees will gain an awareness of the DisCouRSE network and understand how they can both get involved and benefit from its activities. For some this will be ways to enhance their own careers; for some it will be more how they can work with the network to support others and bring systemic change. In addition, this talk will direct those with an interest in specific areas (e.g. competencies, training, management, careers) to other parts of the conference programme where we are involved in more interactive sessions that they can contribute to. Attendees will learn about our flexible fund, the types of submission we are looking for, and how to apply for funding. Prerequisites This talk will not assume any prior knowledge, briefly setting the scene before describing our Network's planned activities at a level suitable for a general audience.

event.title: Running a local RSE call for proposals
event.description:
Abstract In this talk we present a call for proposals at the University of Sheffield aimed at broadening engagement across disciplines. Run in collaboration with our colleagues in the Data Analytics team it provided research active staff with access to up to six months of RSE expertise. The call launched in 2024 and ran again in 2025.
We describe the structure of the call, its target audience, application content and selection process and criteria. Data from the two calls will be presented alongside an assessment of their outcome and a discussion of the lessons learned from their implementation. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes The audience will learn how we ran this call for proposals and get to know what we learn from it. Prerequisites Not skills or knowledge are necessary to understand the talk.

event.title: CapX – .NET Blazor-ing a trail? An(other) operational management tool for RSE groups
event.description:
Abstract Whether you are leading a team of a few RSEs or managing a large department full of all manner of digital research technical professionals, capacity management is an essential activity. That is, knowing what everyone is assigned to work on, at what percentage, and for how long. The “spreadsheet of doom” used to play “Assignment Tetris” was an ineffective tool for the purpose, and so Capacity eXtended (CapX) was developed. However, it didn’t stop there. Frustrated by the lack of frictionless access to good quality data related to people and projects, the CapX data model started to grow, connecting information across the full research lifecycle. CapX now features workload model management for all staff, a competency framework to track development, timesheets, project cost tracking and a secure API so RSEs can build their own tools on top of the database. This walkthrough will demonstrate the features and provide insights into the supporting processes that underpin them. Furthermore, it will discuss the choice of .NET Blazor as its foundation and present as case for why Blazor might be an ideal choice to help diversify your RSE web technology pool. Acknowledgements We acknowledge additional contributions to the CapX code base from Ian Hinder, Andrew Rowley, Chris Lam, Donal Fellows and Maryna Shedzko, all of the RSE department at The University of Manchester. Additional information The format of this submission could be adjusted to a talk and be of shorter or longer length if the schedule requires it. Authors
Event Type Walkthrough In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes The hope is that attendees directly involved in the management of an RSE group will openly discuss with the presenter and others in the session issues and the extent to which CapX might inspire solutions to issues we know are a universal pain in RSE operations management. They can compare feature lists with similar tools in other groups in order to inspire them to adopt one of the existing tools or think about building something themselves, learning from the experiences presented. There is an opportunity to question design choices and or inclusion or exclusion. Highlighting .NET in the walkthrough as a perhaps less familiar technology in RSE circle is important as attendees will be encouraged to consider the diversity in knowledge in their teams around web frameworks and have the opportunity to discuss the choice of Blazor and whether there is any benefit to investigating it in their own groups. Prerequisites The audience should be familiar with how the research environment works and the ways in which RSEs are engaged in project work. As such, they will likely have an appreciation of the issues that may arise from planning and management of this situation which frames the presentation. These issues are introduced in the walkthrough in any case. No detailed technical knowledge is required for the discussion around the technology as commentary will be at a broader level, considering popular alternatives, with any specifics explained.

event.title: RSE perspectives on AI code generation tools: Open discussion and drafting of a position statement
event.description:
Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has already embarked on a significant incursion into the domain of RSEs, impacting all four pillars of Research Software Engineering: development, community, training, and policy.
Do you have a positive vision for a future of Research Software Engineering with GenAI coding tools, or do you feel that there are underappreciated risks? Are you interested in working together as a community of RSEs to shape policy and practice? Whether you have experiences to share, questions to raise, or simply want to listen and learn, you are most welcome at this Birds of a Feather session.
GenAI sits at the intersection of a wide range of issues, making the very idea of 'best practice' troublesome and contentious, or at best strongly context-dependent. Even so, many RSEs feel a responsibility to provide guidance and leadership on the use of these tools.
Moreover, we suspect that many RSEs are, like us, reckoning with what these technologies mean for our own professional futures. How should we be advocating for ourselves, both today and in a future where use of GenAI coding tools may be widespread and normalised?
This session will be split into two 90 minutes halves.
* The first half will be dedicated to sharing experiences and perspectives in small break-out groups focused on topics chosen by participants. * The second half will build on these insights to draft a position statement on the use of GenAI tools in research software.
We feel that RSEs have a unique vantage point on this subject, which enables us to provide authentic and relevant guidance to the wider research community. Our ambition is to develop and publish a document that enjoys broad support among RSEs. Acknowledgements Steve Van Tuyl, Academic Data Science Alliance
Micaela Parker, Academic Data Science Alliance
Rayan Sadeldin, Schmidt Sciences Additional information If there are other submissions that propose something similar, we'd be grateful if the organisers would put us in touch so that we can coordinate, or even possibly combine our efforts if there is significant overlap. Authors
Event Type Birds of a Feather In-Person or Online Delivery Hybrid (Both In-Person and Online Presenters) Outcomes Attendees will have an opportunity to share insights and experiences with GenAI programming tools, learn from each other and form valuable connections. The insights gathered in this session will form the basis of a position statement that will attempt to represent the views of the UK RSE community towards these technologies. Note that "views" does not necessarily imply consensus; we anticipate there being areas of dissensus, which may be worth including in their own right. Attendees who remain for the second half of the session will be directly involved in the drafting of the position statement. Prerequisites There are no prerequisites for this session, other than access to an internet-connected device that you are comfortable typing on.

event.title: Building a dRTP training catalogue: Understanding training requirements, gaps and provision for research software, data and computing infrastructure professionals
event.description:
Abstract As Research Software Engineering has grown rapidly, so too has the availability of open training materials designed for either self-learning or instructor delivery. Developing the wide skill set of an experienced RSE, or indeed a research data or research computing infrastructure professional - a “digital Research Technical Professional” (dRTP) - is time consuming and challenging. Everyone follows, to some extent, a personalised “learning pathway”.
Knowing what dRTPs need to learn at any point in their career is one problem, but knowing what material is available to deliver the skills is a further challenge. This is the focus of this BoF session.
The STEP-UP project (https://step-up.ac.uk) aims to offer training across the dRTP space. To help address this, we’re developing a “training catalogue” in the form of a 3x3 grid covering research software, data and computing infrastructure across beginner, intermediate and advanced skill levels. The initial phase of this work has demonstrated just how much material already exists and how useful a community catalogue of training content could be. It has also highlighted a number of key challenges and questions including how we define beginner, intermediate or advanced training, how is "advanced training" represented and what areas are currently missing in the dRTP training material landscape. We are also increasingly aware of the blurred nature of the boundaries between the categories on both axes.
The session will begin by presenting the current state of the work and then open things up to start what we see as an extremely important community discussion. The presence of a large group of RSEs and other dRTPs makes RSECon the ideal forum to gather feedback and suggestions, develop a co-creation approach to this content and build a community around this work. This will help to ensure that outputs provide the best possible support to dRTPs. Acknowledgements Members of the STEP-UP project involved in this submission would like to acknowledge support from UKRI-EPSRC under grant EP/Y02995X/1. Authors
Event Type Birds of a Feather In-Person or Online Delivery Hybrid (Both In-Person and Online Presenters) Outcomes This session will move forward the discussion around availability and accessibility of technical training materials for dRTPs. It will provide feedback on initial attempts under the STEP-UP project to catalogue dRTP training materials and further contribute to the cataloguing activity. The session will also support planning for how to present the training catalogue to the community and ensure sustainability. Ultimately, the aim is to transition the catalogue from a STEP-UP output to a valuable, sustainable, community maintained resource. Key outcomes will be: a) Community review and feedback on STEP-UP project work to catalogue open source dRTP training materials. b) Initial structure presentation and sustainability plan for the training catalogue. c) Informing attendees about the wide range of existing dRTP training materials and the challenges of developing dRTP skills. d) An opportunity for attendees to align their training strategy with colleagues across institutions and make more effective use of existing resources. Prerequisites There are no technical prerequisites to be able to contribute to or get something out of this session. We feel that there is a place for anyone attending the conference to be able to provide a valuable contribution to this session since everyone has some set of skills that they have learnt somehow! We’re keen to ensure that our audience includes trainers, RSEs and other technical professionals, but also that we have a range of attendees across all levels of experience and a range of dRTP roles. In this context, we see this session as an opportunity for a diverse audience encompassing anyone participating in the conference, both online and in-person, to be able to join a community discussion and make a valuable contribution.

Improving diversity and inclusivity in RSE: From understanding to practical tools.
event.description:
Abstract This workshop invites RSEs, team leaders, and community members to learn more about ongoing diversity and inclusivity work at the UK Software Sustainability Institute (SSI) and gain practical tools and techniques to improve diversity in their own contexts. Firstly, we will present key findings from the Inclusive RSE research project which seeks to understand the experiences of underrepresented groups in RSE and work towards practical solutions. event.title: Record a goose sighting: an introduction to accessibility testing for RSEs
event.description:

Guided by real-world user personas, you will explore a fictional government service for recording goose sightings, and discover how design decisions can create accessibility barriers for some users. You'll then apply what you've learned to search for (and fix!) real accessibility barriers in one of your own projects.
No previous accessibility experience is required, but if you’re comfortable editing a user interface or website, you’ll get more out of the final part of the session.

event.title: Reasonable Performance Computing SIG (SIG-RPC): Help Identify and Document Performance Traps in Research Software
event.description:
Abstract Most research software is written by researchers who are not professionally trained programmers. This often leads to subtle but significant performance pitfalls—small coding choices, such as inefficient data structures, that can have an outsized impact on execution time. Even experienced developers struggle with performance issues, as language- and library-specific nuances are often learned through experience rather than formal documentation. Unreasonably slow research software harms the productivity of the researcher using it and wastes energy and shared resources (like HPC systems), which can harm the productivity of other researchers too.
The Reasonable Performance Computing SIG (SIG-RPC) was founded to build a community around the research, development, and advocacy of software performance best practices. A key part of this effort is curating a knowledge base of common performance traps and profiling tools to help researchers and developers write faster, more efficient code.
This workshop will introduce SIG-RPC and its knowledge base, guiding attendees through the process of contributing performance trap nominations and mini-guides based on their own expertise. Participants will engage in hands-on exercises such as:
* Reviewing existing guides – Are they accessible to a broad audience, including non-experts?
* Submitting new performance traps – Are there common pitfalls in your favourite language or library that haven’t yet been nominated or documented?
* Contributing new guides – Can you document a performance trap from our backlog or your own experience?
All contributions will be published with attribution, helping to expand the community’s collective knowledge and supporting the development of future training materials on software performance best practices. Acknowledgements The Reasonable Performance Computing SIG was founded in late 2024 with the support of Society RSE. Robert Chisholm received a 2025 Software Sustainability Institute fellowship to support the development of this community. Authors

Contributed content will be published in the knowledge-base with attribution, and may be used during the development of future training materials around software performance best practices. Prerequisites This workshop is appropriate for attendees that know any programming language used by researchers (e.g. Python, R, C/C++, etc), regardless of their expertise. The exercises available will suit attendees from novice (e.g. reviewing the accessibility of existing materials) to expert (e.g. proposing or drafting new guidance) .

event.title: Green RSE SIG: Working together to reduce the environmental impact of research software
event.description:

Many funders and research institutions have committed to net zero pledges, that require large scale reductions in emissions, but as yet there is no clear pathway as to how these reductions become achievable.
The Green RSE Special Interest Group is working to (1) identify and promote best practices for environmentally responsible research software, (2) collaborate on solutions that improve the efficiency of research code, reduce energy usage, and incorporate green practices into software lifecycle management, (3) advocate for green policies within research institutions, funding bodies, and broader communities, and (4) champion the role of RSEs in reducing the environmental impact of research software.

The intention this year is to highlight individuals who may not usually present on this but whose initiatives in their institutions can be interesting to the Green RSE community. There will also be an open discussion on the common challenges and opportunities this work brings.
By bringing together a diverse and usually underrepresented group of voices, this session aims to spark discussion, surface ideas, and begin building a strong, connected community of practice around sustainable research software. event.title: AMD GPUs for Scientific Computing: Reviewing the Software Ecosystem & Developer Experience
event.description:
Abstract At present, NVIDIA dominates the consumer and scientific GPU markets with a market share above 80% for discrete GPUs. AMD GPUs look to be the most viable short-term competitor, but just how viable are they for scientific computing right now?
In this talk, we will explore the state of the AMD GPU computing ecosystem and compare it against the NVIDIA ecosystem in terms of usability, library availability, support and performance. These aspects are explored through a publicly available suite of implementations of fundamental GPU algorithms e.g. parallel searches and sorts. These are implemented using both NVIDIAs CUDA and AMDs equivalent, HIP/ROCm.
We will also discuss the developer experience of porting a more substantial code which is representative of a scientific computing application. Through this, feature availability is reviewed, looking at things such as atomic operations. In addition we review the state of AMDs compute library ecosystem, discussing the existence and/or effectiveness of equivalents to Thrust, CUB etc.
Finally, we take a look at the viability of tools which offer automatic conversion of code from CUDA to HIP/ROCm. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes Attendees will learn about some of the key differences between programming for NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. In addition, those with limited GPU development experience may benefit from the suite of GPU primitives, which show commented implementations for common parallel algorithms. Prerequisites This talk will be of most interest to developers who write or are interested in writing GPU code to accelerate their software. It could also be of interest to those in charge of purchasing GPUs to be used for scientific computing.

event.title: Making Software Easy-Build Friendly: Streamlining HPC Software Deployment
event.description:
Abstract Reproducible, maintainable, and scalable software builds are fundamental to high-performance computing (HPC) environments. However, the traditional approach of manually compiling and configuring scientific software is often time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to replicate across systems. This presentation explores how making software EasyBuild-friendly significantly simplifies the process of deploying complex software stacks on HPC systems.
EasyBuild is an open-source framework that automates the building, installation, and management of scientific software on HPCs. By creating EasyBuild “easyconfigs” and optionally writing custom “easyblocks,” users can define builds declaratively—reducing the need for manual intervention and ensuring consistent results across installations. The session will cover key principles for adapting or packaging software to be EasyBuild-friendly, including proper handling of dependencies, versioning, environment modules, and integration with software stack management tools like Lmod.
Through practical examples, we will demonstrate how to convert manual build processes into automated EasyBuild recipes. We will highlight the benefits for both research software engineers and end-users: faster deployment, simplified software stack maintenance, and improved reproducibility. Attendees will also learn how to contribute back to the EasyBuild ecosystem, making their software accessible to a broader HPC audience.
By adopting EasyBuild in research environments, institutions can reduce redundant work, standardize their software environments, and free up valuable researcher time. This talk aims to empower RSEs to leverage EasyBuild not just as users, but as contributors shaping the future of sustainable HPC software deployment. Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery Hybrid (Both In-Person and Online Presenters) Outcomes Attendees will gain a clear overview of how EasyBuild works, including its role in simplifying and automating software installation on HPC systems. They will learn how to make their own software easier to deploy and maintain, with reproducibility and scalability in mind. They will also learn about Improved efficiency and collaboration with their software and opportunities for contribution and community building. Prerequisites A basic understanding of Linux command-line environments is essential. Familiarity with compiling or installing software, particularly in HPC or research computing contexts is beneficial. Some exposure to module systems (e.g., Lmod or Environment Modules) is helpful but not required.

event.title: Collaborative development of a performance analysis methodology
event.description:
Abstract Use cases of computationally intensive resources, such as High-Performance Computing (HPC), are increasingly diversifying with the advent of machine learning and the rise of the digital arts and humanities, while traditional HPC continues to push the boundaries and ask for more capability. This means we have a more demanding and diverse audience of HPC developers, and we therefore want to build a community on robust methods and practices for HPC use. Performance analysis must play an integral role in how developers use their software, because performant software allows researchers to do more research, but also to responsibly use the shared HPC resources economically and ecologically. This talk reports on findings from a series of workshops and investigative works undertaken at Durham University to develop a performance analysis methodology that is broad but nonetheless rigorous. Typically, performance analysis training begins with profiling and tracing tools. However, this can often leave developers using tools to generate performance data but without a strategy of how to systematically analyse this data or navigate through the space of analysis options. We propose a ‘methodology first’ approach, in which our use of tools is informed by our methodology, i.e., we want to plan our analysis and reach for the right tool for the job. It also comprises a clear roadmap of how to start an analysis and what steps to follow one by one.
This methodology at the highest level is based on five performance topics: core, intra-node, inter-node, I/O and GPU. The work to develop this methodology has engaged HPC-focused software engineers to collaboratively design decision trees and metrics to probe these individual performance topics. One outlook of this work is to engage with broader communities to understand how these methodologies can be adapted to incorporate the latest HPC workflows including machine learning. Acknowledgements Funding grant numbers need to be verified. Can this be supplied at a later date? Authors
Event Type Talk In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes We hope that people will gain an understanding of our performance analysis methodology, how this intersects with performance analysis tools and the potential for extending this to workflows which are not ‘traditional’ HPC. We believe this is relevant to the RSE community as we hope to see performance analysis become a core component of research software engineering, with a hope of building performance analysis best practice across the RSE community. Prerequisites This talk is aimed principally at an audience with some prior knowledge of scientific computing, parallel programming or High-Performance Computing (HPC). However, this work also hopes to extend performance analysis methodologies to newer users of intensive compute resources, outside of traditional HPC communities, such as machine learning and digital arts/humanities. We will not assume people are already familiar with performance analysis but some knowledge of HPC software is desirable.

event.title: JAX for Scientific Computing: Bridging the gap between performance, productivity and portability
event.description:
Abstract In this talk, I will discuss the use of the JAX library for solving problems in scientific computing. After a brief discussion of the main features of the library, I will focus on how these features enable researchers to develop more efficient implementations of their scientific models that can run on both CPUs and GPUs and that can interface with machine-learning models seamlessly. I will show examples of open-source JAX-based solvers for a few problems across computational science and engineering and share personal experience of developing software for applications in fluid mechanics and plasma physics. Finally, I will discuss some limitations of the JAX library and issues and shortcomings that I have experienced. event.title: Embedding energy efficiency in computational communities
event.description:
Abstract The Collaborative Computational Projects (CCPs) are a set of communities funded by CoSeC (https://www.cosec.ac.uk/) that develop and maintain a wide range of scientific software. but without information on energy efficiency, it can be difficult for users and developers to make informed choices about the way they write or use that software. Current understanding is limited, and whilst some communities have started developing guidance on energy efficiency, this is often application specific and time consuming for researchers. Our cross-cutting project aims to generalise existing knowledge of sustainable computing and address common challenges across disciplines by:
* Surveying the CCPs to identify common software libraries, such as BLAS and LAPACK, and challenges to improving energy efficiency, * Benchmarking the performance and carbon intensity of these common software libraries and their alternatives, * Using this information to create best practice guidance to allow RSEs to improve the energy efficiency of their software. event.title: Unit Testing in Fortran
event.description:
Abstract Unit testing and testing in general is widely accepted as essential for any reputable modern software. However, it is common to still find Fortran codebases with large communities that contain little to no testing implemented. Where testing has been implemented, this is often in the form of a small suite of end-to-end regression tests. Whilst these regression tests are a great first step, we can do better! There are already several open-source tools to choose from when it comes to unit testing in Fortran, so there is no time like the present to start testing.
In this walkthrough, we will look at how to set up and write unit tests for Fortran code in a subset of the available tools (pFUnit, test-drive and Veggies) using two build systems (CMake and Fortran Package Manager). Key concepts will be explained and pre-written examples provided. Users will also get a chance to try writing their own Fortran unit tests in a pre-configured repository. Examples will cover testing both serial and parallelised Fortran using OpenMP and MPI, highlighting any key differences. To follow along with writing some tests, users will require their own machine. Prior to the session, please follow the instructions within the README.md of this GitHub repository - github.com/UCL-ARC/fortran-unit-testing-exercises. It is particularly important that users have a working version of the pFUnit library installed within their environment prior to the session. This will already be the case if GitHub Codespaces are used. A brief description of the required steps will be provided during the walkthrough. Knowledge of unit testing is desirable but not necessary.

event.title: Observability: A Practical Primer for RSEs
event.description:
Abstract When you distribute and run your software, do you have a good idea of how it's functioning "in the wild"? Do your users have to manually report back to you when they find a bug - and do you have access to the software state when it occurred? How do you know if your application has enough resources when running on a cluster or the cloud, and at what rate it's processing datasets/jobs?
These questions are some of the motivating use cases underpinning observability, which can broadly be defined as using event-driven data (telemetry) to gain insights into the functioning of both software and infrastructure. Observability is useful for troubleshooting issues on production systems, monitoring performance and security, and for tracking key metrics and events happening within a system.
In this introductory walkthrough, I will introduce observability in the context most often used by RSEs - running software in "batch" mode (e.g. running on a cluster) or "server" mode (long-running applications on cloud or workstations). The three main telemetry types will be introduced - metrics, logs, traces - and I will demonstrate how to capture metrics from Python applications in "batch" mode using Microbench (pypi.org/project/microbench) and in "server" mode using OpenTelemetry (opentelemetry.io) and Prometheus (prometheus.io). I will share resources for capturing logs and traces (for later study, in the interests of time). The emphasis will be on simple, practical examples that RSEs can adopt into their own software with minimal fuss. Additional information
Authors
Event Type Walkthrough In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes By the end, participants should gain an understanding of what observability is and its benefits for RSEs, and how to instrument their Python code to capture key metrics such as memory usage and number of requests. An understanding of how to run Docker containers will be needed to fully replicate the examples provided with Prometheus, but the majority of the content won't require this.

event.title: Entity tagging and relation extraction from historical texts using deep learning
event.description:
Abstract The process of assigning metadata to spans of text in order to encode meaning, or “marking up”, has been central to digital humanities practice since before the field had a name. Thousands of person-hours have been devoted to this task, either performing the process entirely manually, or partially assisted by NLP software.
Since the 2010s, deep learning has profoundly impacted NLP, greatly expanding the range of language tasks which can be performed automatically or semi-automatically. Transformers in particular have improved the performance of tasks such as Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Relation Extraction (RE) to the point where it is plausible that markup tasks previously performed by skilled research assistants can, with appropriate training data, be automated or partially automated. The Digital Humanities Institute in Sheffield has been involved in many large scale markup projects over the past twenty-five years and amassed a huge tranche of potential training data for these tasks. To what extent can deep learning models accurately learn and replicate the work of the researchers who first tagged this material in the 2000s and 2010s?
This walkthrough will instruct participants in how to set up and train a transformer model to mark up defendants, crimes and verdicts in text from the Old Bailey Proceedings and correctly identify the relationships between them. It will also explore how to deduce the optimum training strategy for any similar markup task. For example, the number of ground truth human examples required to produce good results, or shortcuts such as using a partially trained transformer to assist a semi-automated workflow.
Ultimately this technology should allow relevant digital humanities projects to be delivered at lower cost and allocate more time and resources to data analysis rather than markup, promoting research excellence. Acknowledgements This walkthrough uses data from the Old Bailey Proceedings Online (https://www.oldbaileyonline.org/), which was funded by the AHRC, ESRC and National Lottery. I am grateful to Dr Zoe Alker (https://www.lancaster.ac.uk/arts-and-social-sciences/people/zoe-alker) and Matthew Groves (https://www.dhi.ac.uk/groves/) for their insight, advice and feedback in preparing it. Authors
Event Type Walkthrough In-Person or Online Delivery In-Person Outcomes The walkthrough will aim to demystify what is possible with entity recognition and relation extraction using current deep learning technology, what is currently not possible, and provide working Python code which demonstrates these methods in action. Programmers will get a full working example of a deep learning model being trained on a corpus of existing marked up material, that model then being used to reproduce the markup scheme on plain text files. This is a process which they can then adapt to their own work on current or future projects. Project managers and scholars will get an understanding of the current possibilities and limitations of deep learning technology for carrying out text markup tasks, and some indication of how these methods can be integrated into a wider project, either existing or prospective. Prerequisites The walkthrough will involve executing Python code in a Google Colab environment, with insight into what is possible with the technology and advice on designing a workflow involving these methods within a wider project. Therefore the session will be of interest to software engineers looking to apply these methods directly to their work, project managers looking to perform text markup tasks more efficiently, and scholars considering a funding bid involving text markup. Software engineers will get more from the walkthrough if they have a strong working knowledge of Python, especially if they are already familiar with deep learning architectures, although the latter will be explained by way of a brief introduction to the libraries involved. Project managers and academics will benefit from a familiarity with digital humanities methodologies, particularly those surrounding text markup, although this is not essential and it is hoped that the walkthrough may prompt new research ideas.

event.title: How to talk to your documents: An introduction to using natural language to query documents with Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
event.description:
Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful, but they have some well-known limitations particularly when interacting with your own documents. LLMs can hallucinate facts, they don't have access to up-to-date or private information, and they can't always explain where their answers come from. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a way to fix some of these problems by letting the model pull in relevant information from external sources before generating a response. This makes answers more accurate, more current, and easier to verify because the model can cite its sources.
In this session, we'll introduce the basics of how RAG works and then walk through building a complete RAG system from scratch using only open-source tools. We'll use Python, along with libraries like Ollama and LangChain, to show how you can build a local document search system, connect it to an LLM, and get better answers without relying on any external APIs. You’ll learn how to index documents, retrieve them effectively, and generate responses.
We’ll also touch on common RAG limitations, such as the importance of data quality and handling large context sizes. Finally, we’ll look at a few advanced techniques to help improve accuracy and performance. By the end, you’ll have a working understanding of what RAG is, how to implement it using open source tools, and how to build and apply your own RAG powered applications to talk to your own documents. Additional information Could also be delivered as a slimmer 30 minute session. Authors
Event Type Walkthrough In-Person or Online Delivery Hybrid (Both In-Person and Online Presenters) Outcomes By the end of the walkthrough, attendees will understand why Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is important and how it helps address key limitations of large language models, such as hallucinations, outdated knowledge, and the inability to cite sources. They will learn how to build a RAG application from scratch using only open-source tools, learning how to load and chunk documents, generate embeddings, index data, template prompts, and generate responses. The session will also highlight how LLMs can be run locally and integrated with domain-specific information without relying on external APIs. Prerequisites Basic knowledge of Python and command line programming would be useful. However the concepts will be accessible to everyone.

event.title: The End of Front-End: Delivering Software via LLMs and the Model Context Protocol
event.description:
Abstract What if the future of software delivery didn’t involve a user interface at all? With the rise of large language models (LLMs), we’re entering a new era where software can be consumed through natural conversation, not clicks. In this walkthrough, I’ll introduce the Model Context Protocol (MCP)—a new way to expose real-time, typed, dynamic data to LLMs, enabling them to act as intelligent, conversational front-ends for research software.
I’ll demonstrate how to build a simple MCP server that exposes live data and commands to an LLM, transforming a traditional API into a human-friendly interaction. Along the way, we’ll look at what problems this approach is suited for, how it compares to conventional apps, and what design patterns are emerging.
This session is designed for data scientists, engineers and researchers curious about combining conversational AI with real-world data and delivery workflows. Authors
Event Type Walkthrough In-Person or Online Delivery Hybrid (Both In-Person and Online Presenters) Outcomes You’ll leave with a clear understanding of what MCP is, why it matters, and how to start experimenting with it in your own projects. Prerequisites Attendees should be familiar with general software engineering concepts and have a working understanding of APIs and LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT or similar tools). No prior experience with MCP is required. Some familiarity with Python will help in following the live demo, but the session will remain accessible to those without general programming experience. Concepts will be explained clearly, with analogies and comparisons to known technologies (such as REST). We aim to keep the walkthrough inclusive to participants from both academic and industrial backgrounds.

Deploying a Web Application with Kubernetes, A Beginner's Guide
event.description:
Abstract The academic world is asking for more web-based software to make research more accessible to both researchers and the public. There are many challenges with writing, maintaining and deploying web services, so how as an RSE can we make this journey easier. Cloud-Native technology (Kubernetes) is a very easy and stable way for researchers to deploy cloud based web applications and can be run on everything from a local laptop, Raspberry Pi or HPC reducing the need for a Cloud provider to run your web apps. This workshop is designed for new starters to Kubernetes who wish to have a practical demonstration of how this technology works and how to apply it in their fields.
We will provide a hands-on tutorial of how:
* To deploy a simple web application via Minikube * To make updates to your website * Kubernetes can automatically recover when there are underlying problems.
This workshop is for RSEs of all career stages who are interested in web applications, DevOps or deployment. The aim is for participants to come away with a working understanding of Kubernetes and the tools needed to continue to work on this in their own time and maybe bring the technology into part of their working practice.
This workshop is run by the Cloud-Native SIG, a new special interest group, working to promote the use of Cloud-Native techology in RSE. Acknowledgements I would like to acknowledge the Software Sustainability Institute for awarding Laura Shemilt a fellowship to start the Cloud Native SIG.
I would like to thanks Alex Lubbock (The Rosalind Franklin Institute) for helping with course design and content and Lewis Sampson (STFC SCD) for his support in setting up this workshop. Authors
Event Type Workshop In-Person or Online Delivery Hybrid (Both In-Person and Online Presenters) Outcomes This session is focussed on the benefits of using Kubernetes, an open-source technology that is well supported and widely used. This technology is used across all sectors and does not have strict legal obligations or high license costs. The key objective of this session is to teach users how they can safely and efficiently deploy their applications on a platform that can be run anywhere, reducing costs and time, freeing up RSEs to do more development work. This session is designed for people who are new to or at beginner level with Kubernetes. However, to fully participate you should have some experience with packaging software and deployment. Ideally you will know and be comfortable with docker and docker-compose. We can provide some pre-reading for the session which is open to access. This workshop is designed to be accessible RSEs at all career levels. Prerequisites No prior experience of Kubernetes required, however you will get most out of this if you are familiar with: docker, docker-compose, (nice to have) desiging web applications. The goal of this session is that you can take away something you can use elsewhere. All software listed is open source and available for Windows, Linux and Mac. For the session you will need to bring a laptop with the following installed: Minikube ( https://minikube.sigs.k8s.io/docs/ ) , Git .All course material and the demo web-application will be made available.

event.title: Supporting digital research infrastructure with software audits: Help us shape good practice.
event.description:
Abstract Research Software Engineers who attend this workshop will crowdsource priorities and good practice for conducting audits that can support risk-mitigation and funding applications for different types of Compute and Data infrastructures. This work is supported by UKRI, who will be attending the session.
In early 2025, UKRI’s Digital Research Infrastructure (DRI) Programme asked the Software Sustainability Institute to conduct a scoping study on the ‘critical software’ for its compute and data infrastructure investments. We interviewed 6 infrastructures and conducted focus groups with the wider DRI staff and user community.
Findings indicated a range of risks to critical software, as well as the benefits of conducting audits on infrastructures to help identify risks and plan for their mitigation. While many of the infrastructures we spoke to had some form of auditing process, we found that audit processes could be better integrated into workflows, with the right support.
In this workshop, we will first present our research findings, hear from UKRI DRI and from ‘audit experts’. We will then break into groups (in person and online) to discuss what should be included in audits for different infrastructures, how best to conduct them, and set priorities for implementation.
Outputs from this workshop will feed into SSI’s work with UKRI DRI in developing new auditing practices.
The UKRI DRI programme team are keen to hear the views of the RSE community, and your early support in this session can help steer this process to the benefit of your work! Acknowledgements Thank you to our interview participants from ARCHER2, Isambard AI, JASMIN, iDAH (Seshat), DARE-UK & PSDI. Thanks also to our focus group participants.
Thank you to Chris York (University of Southampton) and Ed Edmondson (University of Birmingham) for helping us to shape the study with early discussions, and thank you to Stephen Pooley (University of Southampton) for sharing his experience of software risk and audits in industry.
The research underpinning this workshop was funded and supported by the UKRI DRI programme through grant AH/Z000114/1. We worked closely with Sophie Janacek and Richard Gunn from UKRI throughout, who provided access to participants, and helped steer the research. Authors
Event Type Workshop In-Person or Online Delivery Hybrid (Both In-Person and Online Presenters) Outcomes Attendees will learn better ways of doing software audits, learn who else in the community might have similar approaches that could be shared, and have a chance for a wider say in what should be done to support infrastructures moving forward. We will publish a blog post about the major findings of the workshop on the SSI blog to ensure wider dissemination. Prerequisites There are no particular skills required. However, some experience of working with compute and/or data infrastructures (as RSEs tend to have) would be useful so that participants can contribute knowledge and understanding from their own experiences. This workshop would most benefit to people responsible for choice of software and infrastructure on research and research software projects, RSE managers and heads of RSE groups, and managers of digital research infrastructures, as they will be most likely to be applying the techniques discussed in this workshop.
